full_text:
Twelve lovely princesses slept in twelve beds in a locked royal chamber, yet every morning their slippers were found worn into holes as if they had danced all night!

The king promised his kingdom to whoever could solve the mystery in three nights; failure meant the scaffold. Many princes tried, fell into drugged slumber, and were executed.

An old wounded soldier received an invisible cloak from an old woman: "Do not drink the wine they offer you, and pretend to sleep!"

The soldier feigned sleep. At midnight, the eldest princess tapped her bed; it sank into the earth, opening a secret stair. Putting on his invisible cloak, the soldier followed them down through groves of silver trees, gold trees, and diamond trees, breaking a twig from each.

They crossed a subterranean lake in twelve boats rowed by twelve handsome princes, entering an enchanted golden castle where they danced until their satin shoes were shredded!

On the third morning, the soldier stood before the king, showed the silver, gold, and diamond twigs, and produced the golden goblet he had taken.

The princesses confessed the enchantment; the soldier chose the eldest princess as his bride and inherited the crown.
moral: Vigilance, discretion, and presence of mind solve the deepest enchantments.

title: The Old Man and His Grandson
summary: An old grandfather could scarcely walk; his knees trembled, his eyes were dim, and his hands shook so that he spilled soup on the tablecloth....
keywords: the old man and his grandson
full_text:
An old grandfather could scarcely walk; his knees trembled, his eyes were dim, and his hands shook so that he spilled soup on the tablecloth.

Disgusted, his son and daughter-in-law made him sit in the corner behind the stove, feeding him scraps from a cheap earthenware bowl. One day, the bowl broke, and they bought him a rough wooden trough.

One afternoon, the parents saw their four-year-old son fitting little wooden boards together on the floor.

"What are you making, my child?" asked the father lovingly.

The little boy replied: "I am making a little wooden trough for you and mother to eat from when I grow up and you are old!"

The husband and wife looked at each other and burst into tears of shame. They brought the old grandfather back to the master table, ate with him in honor, and never spoke another harsh word to him again.
moral: Treat your aged parents with tender reverence, as you would have your own children treat you.

title: One-Eye, Two-Eyes, Three-Eyes
summary: Little Two-Eyes was despised by her sisters One-Eye and Three-Eyes because she looked like ordinary humans. They gave her rags and crusts....
full_text:
Little Two-Eyes was despised by her sisters One-Eye and Three-Eyes because she looked like ordinary humans. They gave her rags and crusts.

A wise woman gave her a magical goat: saying "Little goat, bleat, little table spread!" produced a golden feast.

When the cruel sisters discovered the secret and slaughtered the goat, Two-Eyes buried its entrails before the house.

From the earth sprang a magnificent tree with leaves of silver and apples of solid gold! The proud sisters could not pluck a single apple—the branches leaped away. But when Two-Eyes reached out, the golden apples bent into her hand.

A noble knight rode by, fell in love with her gentle modesty, and took her to his castle, while the tree followed her and planted itself outside her palace window!
moral: Those despised for being normal and gentle are blessed with golden fruit and true love.

Grethel the cook roasted two fat partridges for her master's guest. Tempted by the savory aroma, she tasted a wing; then the other; then both birds were eaten completely, washed down with fine wine!

When the guest arrived, Grethel whispered: "Flee! My master invited you only to slice off both your ears with his carving knife!"

The terrified guest ran for his life. Grethel ran to her master: "Master! Your guest has stolen both roasted partridges and run away!"

The master ran after him with his carving knife, shouting: "Just give me one! Just give me one!" while the guest ran faster, thinking he wanted one of his ears!
moral: Audacious lies to cover greed create comical panics.

full_text:
There was once a king's son who went out into the world full of thoughtful sorrow, reflecting upon the vanity of earthly pomp and the burdens of worldly crowns. Walking across lonely hills and simple meadows, he met a poor old man with silver hair sitting upon a stone, sharing a dry crust with wild birds that flocked to his weathered hand.

The prince sat beside the gentle wanderer and asked, "Father, why do you look so serene when you possess neither gold nor roof against the night?"

The old man smiled softly and answered, "My child, true wealth is not measured in jewels that rust or palaces that crumble to dust. He who walks in humility, seeks neither praise nor vanity, and opens his hand to the suffering, finds that the simplest path leads straight to heaven."

Deeply moved by the elder's peace, the prince cast aside his velvet mantle, clad himself in a plain coarse coat, and walked among the villages, nursing the sick, soothing the broken-hearted, and asking for nothing in return. When his earthly journey reached its evening, celestial light shone upon the peaceful meadow where he lay, and gentle choruses welcomed him into enduring bliss, proving that purity of spirit and quiet love outshine all the crowns of kings.
moral: A humble heart that shares even the smallest crust in love attains true peace and eternal joy.

A young tailor, cheerful of spirit and bold of heart, journeyed deep into a vast forest where towering oaks shut out the sun. As twilight fell, he found refuge inside an underground vault, where an ancient dwarf with a snowy beard stood guarding wonders beyond mortal imagination.

Beneath crystal arches sat a magnificent glass coffin, glowing with warm radiance. Gazing through the clear crystal, the tailor beheld an extraordinarily beautiful maiden lying in enchanted slumber, adorned in silk with golden tresses flowing over her shoulders. Beside her stood miniature castles and enchanted towns sealed within glass vessels.

To release her from the wicked sorcerer's binding spell, the tailor had to overcome ferocious subterranean beasts and break the enchanted seal with fearless devotion. Undaunted by terrifying shadows, he shattered the dark runes. The glass lid swung open, and the lovely maiden awakened with a joyous breath.

She revealed herself to be a wealthy count's daughter imprisoned by an envious wizard. In gratitude for his steadfast valor, she offered him her hand, and the enchanted miniature realm expanded into a flourishing, joyful estate where they ruled in harmony and kindness for all their days.
moral: Courage and an upright spirit can break the darkest enchantments and restore beauty to the light.

full_text:
Lazy Harry was so exceedingly fond of rest that his greatest trial in life was driving his single goat out to pasture every morning. He would stretch upon the grass and sigh, "Ah, what weary work it is to watch this restless beast all day long! If only I had a wife with a goat of her own, she could pasture mine as well, and I might sleep until noon."

With this grand plan in mind, Harry courted Fat Trina, whose father owned a healthy goat. The match was struck, and the two lazy souls wed with great rejoicing. But soon Trina complained bitterly that her ankles ached from walking the pasture.

"Listen, Harry," proposed Trina. "Let us trade our two goats to neighbor Heinz for a beehive! Bees take care of themselves, fly out into the blossoms without driving, make sweet honey without our labor, and need no tending at all."

Harry marveled at her genius. They traded the goats and set the hive near the window. Yet before the first drop of honey could be enjoyed, the pair quarreled over who would stir the pot. Trina brandished her wooden hazel stick in passionate argument, accidentally striking the hive and overturning it entirely into the mud. The furious bees swarmed, stinging them both soundly, leaving the idle dreamers without honey, without goats, and nursing painful lumps as a reminder of their grand follies.
moral: Endless schemes to avoid honest toil usually collapse under the weight of their own foolishness.

full_text:
There was once a king whose daughter fell gravely ill, and the physicians declared she could only be restored to health by eating apples from a miraculous tree. A poor peasant's youngest son, Hans, whom everyone mocked as simple, carried a basket of these golden apples to the palace, where they cured the princess completely.

The ungrateful king, unwilling to give his daughter to a lowly lad, set an impossible condition: "You shall not marry my daughter until you bring me a golden feather plucked from the tail of the terrifying Griffin who dwells at the edge of the world."

Hans bravely set out on the perilous journey. Along the way, he met a master of a lake who could not cross passengers without endless rowing, a king whose fountain had run dry of wine, and another whose tree of gold no longer bore fruit. Hans promised to find answers for each from the mythical Griffin.

Reaching the Griffin's mountain lair, Hans found the beast's kind-hearted wife, who hid him beneath the bed. When the Griffin returned home, hungry and grumbling, the woman gently pulled a golden feather from his tail each time he fell asleep, eliciting the secret answers to the riddles Hans had gathered.

Armed with three golden feathers and the answers, Hans returned. He revealed the toad beneath the dry fountain, the mouse gnawing the golden tree's root, and taught the boatman how to pass his oars to the next traveler. When the jealous king sought the Griffin's hoard for himself, the boatman thrust the oars into his hands, leaving the greedy monarch to row across the dark river forever, while Hans married the princess in everlasting joy.
moral: Quick wits, humble courage, and keen listening conquer monsters that brute force cannot overcome.

Strong Hans was stolen as a baby along with his mother by a band of cruel robbers and locked inside a deep mountain cave. As Hans grew, drinking goat's milk and eating wild roots, his strength increased tenfold, until even the stoutest oak could not withstand his grip.

When Hans reached eighteen years of age, he picked up a gigantic iron club and demanded that the robbers set his mother free. When they drew their blades, Hans swung his iron bar, routing the entire band with mighty sweeps and shattering the cave's heavy stone doors.

Returning his mother safely to his long-grieving father, Hans embarked on adventures across the realm. He joined forces with Fir-Twister and Rock-Splitter, two giants of great renown. Together they ventured into an enchanted subterranean castle to rescue a captured princess from an ancient mountain demon.

When the companions betrayed Hans and abandoned him in the abyss, Hans refused to despair. Using his wits and an enchanted ring he won from the underworld spirit, he summoned magical birds that carried him to the upper world. He confronted the false companions, rescued the grateful princess, and proved that a clean conscience and iron loyalty are mightier than any treacherous scheme.
moral: True strength is forged through loyalty to family and justice against tyranny.

full_text:
A poor, honest peasant arrived at the pearly gates of heaven on the very same morning as a wealthy, celebrated nobleman. When the nobleman approached, heavenly trumpets sounded, angels sang glorious hymns, and celestial gates swung wide in grand celebration.

The peasant stepped forward next, but he was admitted quietly, with gentle smiles from the gatekeeper but without brass horns or grand pageantry. The peasant stood softly in the heavenly courtyard, feeling a brief tremor of worldly doubt, wondering why rich lords were heralded with such thunder while humble plowmen entered in silence.

Saint Peter walked over to him, resting a warm, benevolent hand upon his shoulder. "My son," whispered Peter, "do not misunderstand what you have witnessed. Poor, honest peasants like yourself enter the kingdom of heaven every hour of every day; your steadfast goodness is familiar and beloved in our midst. But a wealthy lord who manages to live righteously, resist greed, and cross this threshold is so rare an arrival that all heaven rejoices when one is saved!"

Hearing this, the peasant chuckled with warm delight, understanding the divine humor and justice, and strolled happily into paradise to enjoy unending peace.
moral: True heavenly celebration welcomes every soul according to the rarity and quiet trials of its journey.

title: Lean Lisa
summary: Lean Lisa had an entirely different disposition from Lazy Harry; she was constantly restless, thrifty to a fault, and worried incessantly about how to amass a greater fortune. She...
full_text:
Lean Lisa had an entirely different disposition from Lazy Harry; she was constantly restless, thrifty to a fault, and worried incessantly about how to amass a greater fortune. She drove her poor husband Long Lenz from dawn to dusk, scolding him for every crumb he dropped and every minute he rested.

One evening, as they sat by the dim hearth, Lisa began to calculate future gains: "If we gather three silver pieces, we shall buy a young calf. The calf will grow into a cow; the cow will give rich milk and bear another calf, and soon we shall have a grand herd that fills the pasture."

"Splendid," said Lenz. "And when the herd multiplies, the boys can milk them and drink sweet cream."

"Drink cream?" shrieked Lisa, her eyes flashing fire. "Never! Do you think we raise cattle for silly children to guzzle down our profits? Every drop of cream shall be churned into butter and sold at the town market!"

"Come now, wife," Lenz reasoned, "the children must have their share."

Furious that her husband dared dispute the distribution of milk from a cow that did not yet exist, Lisa seized the heavy hearth-broom and struck him across the shoulders. Lenz caught the stick, and they scuffled across the cottage, knocking over their only water pitcher and scattering the firewood. When the dust settled, both sat bruised, cold, and exhausted, possessing neither calf nor cream, but only the bitter folly of fighting over castles in the air.
moral: Unbridled greed and arguing over imaginary possessions destroy present peace.

title: The Hut in the Forest

full_text:
A poor woodcutter lived on the edge of a deep forest with his wife and three daughters. One day, the eldest daughter was sent into the woods carrying dinner to her father, but mistaking the trail of millet he had scattered, she wandered deep into the thickets until night fell.

She spotted a solitary light shining from an old thatched hut. Knocking at the door, she was greeted by an elderly grey-haired man sitting at a rustic table, while around him lay an old speckled hen, a red cock, and a spotted cow. The girl asked for food and shelter. The old man asked his animals if they agreed, and they clucked and mooed their consent. The girl ate heartily of the porridge, but offered not a crumb to the faithful creatures, nor did she bid them goodnight. When she went upstairs to sleep, the floor gave way, dropping her into a dark cellar.

The second daughter suffered the exact same fate on the following day, selfishly feeding only herself and ignoring the beasts.

On the third day, the youngest daughter ventured out. Arriving at the hut, she greeted the old man with gentle warmth, stroked the hen and the cock, and gave the spotted cow a generous handful of sweet hay. She shared her supper with all three beasts before tasting a single spoonful herself, and made sure their water trough was filled.

When she awoke next morning, the tiny hut had transformed into a dazzling royal palace of marble and gold! The old man was revealed to be an enchanted prince, transformed by a sorcerer until a maiden of pure compassion should appear who treated beasts with the same loving honor as kings. The cellar opened to release the older sisters, who were sent to learn humility, while the youngest married the prince and lived in boundless harmony.
moral: Kindness shown to the smallest and humblest creatures unlocks the door to genuine blessing.

title: Sharing Joy and Sorrow
summary: A stubborn and ill-tempered tailor married a clever, spirited woman and immediately declared: "In this household, wife, we shall share joy and sorrow equally. When I eat tasty roas...
full_text:
A stubborn and ill-tempered tailor married a clever, spirited woman and immediately declared: "In this household, wife, we shall share joy and sorrow equally. When I eat tasty roasts and drink fine wine, that is my joy, and you shall share in my pleasure by watching me eat. When you fail to obey my slightest whim, that is my sorrow, and you shall share in it by feeling my measuring yard across your shoulders!"

The clever wife said nothing, but bided her time. One morning, the tailor ordered three plump sausages fried for his supper and left for the village. The wife cooked the sausages to perfection, but realizing her husband's intolerable cruelty, she sat down and ate two of them with relish, leaving only the smallest skin behind.

When the tailor returned and saw the empty plate, he flew into a rage: "Where are my two sausages, wretched woman?"

"Husband," she replied sweetly, "I was sharing your joy! You always taught me that joy must be shared. Watching you eat gave me such radiant happiness that I thought experiencing the taste directly would double our marital joy!"

Furious, the tailor seized his measuring yard, but the wife quickly slipped behind the heavy kitchen cupboard, causing him to stumble over his own stool and overturn a kettle of cold dye upon his trousers. Shivering and soaked in indigo, he sat on the floor, while she laughed: "Now, beloved husband, we can truly share your sorrow, for your clothes are ruined, but your wit has at last been sharpened!" title: The Willow-Wren
summary: Once upon a time, the birds of the air grew tired of having no ruler and resolved to hold a contest: whichever bird could fly highest into the sky should be crowned king of all win...
full_text:
Once upon a time, the birds of the air grew tired of having no ruler and resolved to hold a contest: whichever bird could fly highest into the sky should be crowned king of all winged creatures.

On a bright summer morning, eagles, hawks, storks, and songbirds gathered in a vast meadow. At the signal, they all launched into the heavens. The smaller birds soon wearied and dropped back to earth, leaving only the mighty Eagle soaring higher and higher, brushing the very clouds. Convinced of his victory, the Eagle cried out in triumph, "I am your king!"

Suddenly, from beneath the Eagle's breast feathers, a tiny Willow-Wren popped out. He had hitched a ride unseen, and now fluttered another twenty feet into the blue, chirping proudly, "King am I! King am I!"

The birds below were outraged at this trickery. They refused to crown the little cheat unless he could prove his worth by sinking deepest into the earth. The wren hopped into a mouse-hole and refused to come out. The birds set the Owl to guard the hole, but the Owl nodded off in the morning sun, allowing the nimble wren to escape into the hazel hedges.

To this day, the Willow-Wren is called Kinglet, chirping defiantly from deep within the briars, reminding all creatures that size alone does not determine the dignity of a ruler.
moral: True sovereignty is earned not by mere size or empty flight, but through resourcefulness and integrity.

title: The Sole

full_text:
The fishes of the sea, having lived in wild confusion for centuries, decided they needed a king to maintain order and dispense justice in the deep waters. They agreed that whichever fish could swim fastest through the waves to the distant sandbar should be proclaimed sovereign.

The Pike, the Salmon, the Herring, and all the finned creatures lined up in the blue swell. At the signal, they darted forward with tremendous speed. The nimble Herring outpaced them all, shooting like a silver arrow through the foam and touching the sandbar first.

The Sole, a flat, boastful fish who had lagged far behind, arrived breathless and asked with arrogant disdain, "Who is it that has won the crown?"

"The Herring! The Herring!" cried the joyous assembly of fishes.

"The naked Herring?" sneered the Sole, twisting his mouth in bitter mockery and curling his lip. "That scrawny little fellow our king? What an absurd joke!"

Because of this venomous grimace of envy and disrespect, the Sole's mouth remained twisted to one side forever, his eyes shifted awkwardly to the upper surface, and he was condemned to crawl flat upon the ocean floor, bearing the permanent mark of his jealous spite.
moral: Envy and jealous mockery disfigure the soul and leave an indelible mark.

title: The Bittern and the Hoopoe

full_text:
In ancient times, before they took their avian forms, the Bittern and the Hoopoe were mortal herdsmen pasturing cattle in adjacent meadows.

The man who became the Bittern had rich, fat cows, but he was indolent and loved his afternoon nap. While he slumbered beneath the alders, his cows strayed into treacherous bogs and sank into the mire. When he awoke and found his herd missing, he rushed wildly among the reeds, crying in desperate mournful tones, "Come back! Come back!" transformed into a marsh bird whose hollow, booming cry echoes across the fens to this day.

The man who became the Hoopoe, on the other hand, was assigned lean, unruly heifers that sprinted in all directions. He had to run up hills and down valleys, waving his staff, shouting and whistling until his breath gave out: "Up, up, up! Heifers, back!" In the end, he was changed into the crested Hoopoe, whose distinctive call "Up-up-up" still sounds from sunny glades, forever echoing the frantic cries of a herdsman trying to keep his wandering herd in line.
moral: Neglect of duty brings lamentation, while diligent care preserves honor.

full_text:
A couple of centuries ago, an owl strayed into a town barn by mistake, seeking shelter from the blinding sunlight. When the servant went to fetch hay in the afternoon, he saw two huge fiery eyes glowing in the dark rafters and fled screaming that a terrifying demon had invaded the village.

The mayor assembled the town council, armed with pitchforks, scythes, and heavy clubs. Peeking through the door, the trembling villagers saw the bird blink its round eyes and heard it snap its beak with a quiet click. Panic gripped the crowd. "It is a monster from the abyss!" shouted the mayor. "If it escapes, it will devour our children and ruin our crops!"

Rather than confront the harmless creature, the heroic town elders decided there was only one safe course: they barricaded the barn tightly and set fire to the four corners. The flames devoured the timber, the wheat, and the hay, reducing the proudest building in the valley to smoldering ashes.

Just as the roof collapsed, the owl spread its soft wings, soared silently through the smoke into the open blue sky, and perched on a distant oak, unharmed and deeply amused, leaving the foolish villagers weeping over their self-inflicted ruin.
moral: Ignorance and irrational panic turn harmless wonders into terrifying monsters.

title: The Moon
summary: In ancient days, there was a land where the night was pitch-dark, for no moon shone in their heavens. Four wanderers journeyed to another country and saw a radiant silver sphere ha...
full_text:
In ancient days, there was a land where the night was pitch-dark, for no moon shone in their heavens. Four wanderers journeyed to another country and saw a radiant silver sphere hanging from the bough of an oak tree, shedding soft, beautiful light across the fields.

Learning that the villagers paid a small tax to keep the oil lamp burning, the four greedy travelers stole the silver moon, carried it back to their own land, and hung it in a tall tree, demanding payment from their neighbors for its light.

As the four men grew old and passed away one by one, each demanded that a quarter of the moon be cut off and buried in his coffin. When the last man died, the sky was completely dark once more, while down in the underworld, the four quarters reunited, shedding light upon the departed souls.

The spirits of the underworld awoke, mistaking the light for daylight, and began drinking, singing, and bowling in a riotous tavern brawl. Hearing the commotion shaking the earth, Saint Peter rode down on his steed to restore order. He calmed the riotous dead, took the silver moon in his hands, and carried it high into the celestial vault, hanging it forever in the open night sky where its gentle light can bless all living beings without price or ownership.
moral: Natural wonders and light belong to all humanity, not to be hoarded by selfish pride.

title: The Duration of Life
summary: When the Creator created the world and appointed the years of life to each living creature, the Donkey came first and was offered thirty years. The Donkey sighed, "Lord, thirty yea...
full_text:
When the Creator created the world and appointed the years of life to each living creature, the Donkey came first and was offered thirty years. The Donkey sighed, "Lord, thirty years of carrying heavy sacks to the mill, being beaten with sticks, and eating thistles is far too weary a burden. Spare me half of them!" And eighteen years were taken away.

Next came the Dog, who was offered thirty years. "Lord," wept the Dog, "running, barking at thieves, losing teeth, and lying stiffly in corners is too long a misery. Give me fewer!" And twelve years were removed.

Next came the Monkey, who begged for relief from thirty years of making silly faces to amuse ungrateful spectators, and ten years were lifted from him.

Finally came Man, proud and joyful, who was offered thirty years. "Thirty years?" protested Man. "Just when I build my house and plant my fields, I must depart? Give me more!"

The Creator granted him the eighteen years refused by the donkey, the twelve years refused by the dog, and the ten years refused by the monkey.

Thus it is that Man lives his first thirty years in human vigor and joy. Then follow the donkey years, bearing heavy burdens of household toil; then the dog years, sitting watchful in the corner, grumbling and guarding; and finally the monkey years, silly and weak, mocked by the young as age takes its toll.
moral: Every stage of life has its appointed character; peace comes from accepting each season with grace.

title: Death's Messengers
summary: In ancient times, a robust young giant was traveling along the highway when he encountered Death sitting exhausted by the roadside, having been beaten in a duel with a mighty champ...
full_text:
In ancient times, a robust young giant was traveling along the highway when he encountered Death sitting exhausted by the roadside, having been beaten in a duel with a mighty champion. The compassionate young man revived Death with fresh spring water and helped him to his feet.

In gratitude, Death promised: "I cannot spare you when your appointed hour strikes, for my duty is universal. But this I swear: I will never come upon you unawares. I shall send my messengers ahead to announce my coming, so you may be ready."

Years passed into decades. The young man grew into a prosperous citizen, enjoying health, wine, and laughter. But gradually, his hair turned silver, his eyesight dimmed, his joints began to ache with winter frost, and a dull ringing settled in his ears. Yet he remained carefree, thinking, "Death has not arrived; he has not sent his heralds!"

At last, a cold tap touched his shoulder, and Death stood before him. "It is time," Death declared.

"False friend!" cried the man. "Did you not swear to send messengers before taking me?"

"Foolish man," answered Death softly. "Have I not sent them every single year? Did not gray hair, failing vision, aching bones, and heavy breath knock upon your door? Every pain, every wrinkle, every weary step was my messenger whispering: prepare your house, for the evening draws near." The man bowed his head in humble understanding, and accompanied his guide into peace.
moral: The aches and changes of aging are gentle warnings to prepare the soul with wisdom and kindness.

title: Master Pfriem
summary: Master Pfriem was a cobbler so exceedingly irritable and fault-finding that nothing on earth could ever please him. If a shoe had five stitches, he complained it lacked six; if the...
full_text:
Master Pfriem was a cobbler so exceedingly irritable and fault-finding that nothing on earth could ever please him. If a shoe had five stitches, he complained it lacked six; if the leather was soft, he insisted it should be stiff; and if the apprentice was diligent, Pfriem cursed him for being slow.

When Pfriem died, he climbed up to heaven's gate and knocked loudly. Saint Peter opened the gate and warned him: "Master Pfriem, you may enter heaven, but remember this: you must keep your mouth shut. Here you must find no faults, critique no angel, and meddle in no divine affairs, or you will be cast out."

Pfriem promised to behave, but within an hour his fingers twitched with irritation. He saw two angels carrying a great beam; they held it crosswise instead of lengthwise, making it hard to pass through the golden portal. Pfriem bit his lip until blood flowed, trying to restrain himself.

Next, he saw a team of celestial horses pulling an overloaded wagon of hay, and the driver sat backward. This was too much for the compulsive fault-finder. "Hey, you clumsy blockhead!" shouted Pfriem at the top of his lungs. "Who ever saw horses harnessed that way? Turn your cart around, you foolish knave!"

At that instant, Saint Peter appeared, took Master Pfriem by the collar, and gently led him outside the gates, saying, "Go find a kingdom where perfection needs your corrections, for heaven requires only gratitude and peace."
moral: Those who spend their lives finding fault in others must learn that silence and grace are higher virtues.

title: The Goose-Girl (Die Gänsemagd)
summary: A beautiful royal princess was betrothed to a king's son in a distant land. When the time came for her bridal journey, her loving mother gave her a handkerchief marked with three d...
full_text:
A beautiful royal princess was betrothed to a king's son in a distant land. When the time came for her bridal journey, her loving mother gave her a handkerchief marked with three drops of maternal blood for protection, and a magnificent talking horse named Falada. She was accompanied by a treacherous maid-in-waiting.

On the long journey across parched plains, the princess asked the maid to fetch her a cup of water from the brook. The maid arrogantly refused: "I will not serve you any longer; climb down and drink yourself!" In her distress, the princess dropped her handkerchief into the stream, losing her mother's blessing.

Taking advantage of her weakness, the cruel maid forced the princess to trade dresses, switch horses, and swear a solemn oath beneath the open sky never to reveal the betrayal to any mortal living soul. At the palace, the false bride was received in grand splendor, while the real princess was sent into the meadows to herd geese alongside a boy named Conrad.

Fearing the horse would speak, the wicked maid ordered Falada beheaded. But the gentle princess begged the knacker to nail the horse's head over the dark city gateway, where she passed every morning. As she walked beneath, she sighed: "Alas, Falada, hanging there!" and the horse answered: "Alas, young queen, how sad your share! If your dear mother only knew, her loving heart would break in two."

Conrad grew furious when the princess untied her golden hair in the meadow, gleaming like the sun, and the wind blew his hat away whenever he tried to steal a strand. He complained to the old king, who observed the girl and saw her deep sorrow.

When the king questioned her, she wept that she had sworn never to tell her grief to any mortal. The wise old king said: "If you cannot speak to me, pour out your heart to the iron stove in the corner."

The princess crawled into the warm iron stove and poured forth her whole tragic story of treachery and suffering. The king, listening through the flue pipe outside, heard every word. He clothed her in royal silk, summoned a magnificent feast, and asked the false bride what punishment a traitor deserved. The wicked maid condemned herself out of her own mouth, and the true queen was restored to her rightful throne beside her joyful prince.
moral: True nobility cannot be stolen, and the quiet truth will always triumph over deceit.

title: The Young Giant
summary: A country peasant had a son no bigger than a thumb, who refused to grow regardless of how much bread he ate. One day, a colossal giant passed through the field, scooped up the tiny...
full_text:
A country peasant had a son no bigger than a thumb, who refused to grow regardless of how much bread he ate. One day, a colossal giant passed through the field, scooped up the tiny lad, and carried him to the mountaintops, nourishing him on wild giant's pine-sap and bear milk.

Within a few years, the little boy had grown into an astonishing titan whose shoulders could shake mountains and who could uproot giant oak trees with a casual tug of his hand. He returned to his father's cottage, but his enormous size terrified his parents, who could not afford to feed such an appetite.

The young giant set out into the wide world to seek employment. He hired himself out to a greedy blacksmith, asking as his only wage: two hearty kicks against the smith's backside when the year was completed. The smith laughed, thinking it a jest, but soon realized his new apprentice could hammer an entire anvil into the ground with one strike.

When the year ended, the terrified blacksmith tried to hide and cheat the giant out of his wage, setting fierce traps and throwing boulders from cliffs. But the young giant brushed off the rocks like grains of dust. He returned to the forge, administered the agreed-upon kick that sent the dishonest smith flying over the village steeple, and strode off into the world, an unstoppable champion of fairness and honest contracts.
moral: Great strength is meant to uphold justice and humble arrogance, not to bully the weak.

title: The Gnome (Dat Erdmänneken)
summary: A king had three beautiful daughters who were stolen away into a deep subterranean cavern by an evil enchanter. Three brave huntsman brothers set out to rescue them, scouring the d...
full_text:
A king had three beautiful daughters who were stolen away into a deep subterranean cavern by an evil enchanter. Three brave huntsman brothers set out to rescue them, scouring the dark forests until they found an ancient castle where a tiny gray gnome dwelled beneath the kitchen flagstones.

The gnome showed them the yawning mouth of an abyss leading deep into the center of the earth. The two older brothers took fright at the dizzying depths and refused to descend. Only the youngest brother, steadfast and courageous, climbed into the wicker basket and was lowered down into the dark chasm.

At the bottom, he fought through enchanted serpents and fire-breathing dragons, rescuing all three princesses and collecting the magnificent golden apples that symbolized their royal heritage. He placed the maidens in the basket one by one and signaled his brothers to haul them up.

When it came time for the youngest brother to be raised, he wisely placed a heavy boulder in the basket instead of himself. As expected, his envious brothers cut the rope halfway up, hoping to kill him and claim the royal brides for themselves.

Trapped in the underworld, the abandoned hero wandered until he found a wounded griffin chick. He fed the young bird and protected it from a ravenous serpent. In gratitude, the mother griffin carried the loyal youth upon her back through the subterranean clouds up into the sunlight.

He presented the princesses with their golden apples, unmasked his treacherous brothers, and took the hand of the youngest princess in a joyous wedding celebrated throughout the land.
moral: True brotherhood is tested in adversity; faithful integrity rises above cowardly treachery.

title: The King of the Golden Mountain
summary: A merchant ruined by shipwrecks was walking through his barren fields when an eerie black dwarf offered him boundless wealth in exchange for the first thing that brushed against hi...
keywords: the king of the golden mountain
full_text:
A merchant ruined by shipwrecks was walking through his barren fields when an eerie black dwarf offered him boundless wealth in exchange for the first thing that brushed against his leg when he returned home. Thinking of his faithful hound, the merchant agreed. But to his horror, his little seven-year-old son ran out to embrace his knees.

Years later, when the time came to surrender the boy, the lad stood inside a circle of holy chalk, and the dwarf could not touch him. Placed adrift in a wooden skiff upon the river, the youth floated across the endless sea until he landed on the shores of the enchanted Golden Mountain.

There he found an enchanted snake that begged him to endure three nights of silent torment from dark phantoms to break her curse. The brave youth endured the spectral blows without uttering a single groan. On the third morning, the serpent transformed into a radiant queen, who made him King of the Golden Mountain and bore him a lovely child.

Longing to visit his aged father, the young king returned to his native land, bearing a ring that could transport him anywhere—provided he did not demand his wife accompany him against her will. Overcome by pride at a feast, he invoked her presence, breaking the pact. The queen took the child and the ring while he slept and vanished back to the Golden Mountain.

Undaunted, the king journeyed on foot for twelve long years. Along the way, he encountered three squabbling giants and cleverely obtained their three magical treasures: a sword that decapitated enemies at a word, a cloak of invisibility, and boots that could travel a hundred leagues in a single stride.

Arriving at the Golden Mountain just as the unfaithful queen was celebrating her wedding to another, the invisible king revealed the truth, drove the pretender from the throne, and reclaimed his rightful sovereignty with dignity and justice.
moral: Steadfast loyalty overcomes broken oaths, and magical gifts aid the righteous heart.

title: The Raven
summary: A queen in a fit of impatient temper wished that her crying baby girl were a raven so she might fly away. No sooner had the rash words been spoken than the infant transformed into...
full_text:
A queen in a fit of impatient temper wished that her crying baby girl were a raven so she might fly away. No sooner had the rash words been spoken than the infant transformed into a black raven and flew out of the window into a dark, impenetrable pine forest.

Years later, a wandering huntsman heard the voice of the raven pleading from an ancient oak: "I am a king's daughter under an evil enchantment. If you wish to save me, journey to the castle of Stromberg on the Glass Mountain. But beware: an old woman will offer you wine and sweetmeats; touch neither, or you will fall into a fatal sleep!"

The huntsman swore to rescue her, but at the cottage near the mountain, the witch deceived him into drinking a single drop of drugged wine. For three consecutive days, the huntsman fell into a deep slumber just as the raven flew past in her carriage. On the third day, the raven left him a loaf of inexhaustible bread, a piece of meat that never diminished, a bottle of endless wine, and a golden ring inscribed with her name.

Awakening in agony of soul, the huntsman wept for his weakness and set out on foot to find the Glass Mountain. He walked for years, overcoming fierce giants and traversing wild continents. With the aid of a magical steed and enchanted climbing hooks, he scaled the sheer, slippery wall of glass.

Entering the golden castle, he dropped the ring into the princess's wine goblet. Recognizing the token of his enduring devotion, the restored princess embraced him with tears of joy, and they were wed in radiant splendor before the assembled realm.
moral: Unwavering devotion can scale mountains of glass and undo the rash curses of anger.

title: The Peasant's Wise Daughter
summary: A poor peasant dug up a golden mortar in a field given to him by the king. His clever daughter warned him: "Father, do not present the mortar to the king without the pestle, or he...
full_text:
A poor peasant dug up a golden mortar in a field given to him by the king. His clever daughter warned him: "Father, do not present the mortar to the king without the pestle, or he will accuse you of keeping it." The father did not listen, and true to her words, the suspicious king threw him into the dungeon.

Hearing the peasant lament, "Alas, had I but listened to my daughter!" the curious king summoned the maiden. Intrigued by her reputation for wit, he presented her with a famous riddle: "Come to my palace neither naked nor clad, neither riding nor walking, neither on the road nor off the road; if you succeed, I shall take you as my queen."

The wise daughter wrapped herself in a large fishing net, tied the net to a donkey's tail so that one toe dragged along the rut of the road while the other hovered in the air, and thus arrived at the palace. Delighted by her brilliance, the king made her his queen.

They lived happily until one day the king made an unjust ruling in a dispute between two peasants over a newborn foal. The wise queen secretly advised the wronged peasant to fish in dry dust, prompting the king to realize his error. Angry that his wife had outsmarted his royal judgment, the king banished her, allowing her to take only "the dearest and most precious thing" from the palace.

That night, the queen gave the king a sleeping potion, had him placed in a gentle carriage, and conveyed him to her humble cottage. When the king awoke on her straw bed, he cried, "Where am I?"

"Beloved husband," she replied with a tender smile, "you permitted me to take what was dearest and most precious to me from your palace, and on earth there is nothing dearer to my heart than you." Touched to tears by her love and wisdom, the king embraced her, returned to his throne with her at his side, and ruled wisely under her counsel for the rest of his days.
moral: Clever insight and heartfelt devotion are more valuable than gold or royal pride.

title: Old Hildebrand
summary: A cunning village priest and a deceitful peasant woman wished to spend days dining on roasted capons and drinking sweet cider without her husband, Old Hildebrand, getting in the wa...
full_text:
A cunning village priest and a deceitful peasant woman wished to spend days dining on roasted capons and drinking sweet cider without her husband, Old Hildebrand, getting in the way. The priest advised the woman to pretend to be gravely ill and announce that she could only be cured if her husband made a long barefoot pilgrimage to a distant mountain shrine.

Simple Hildebrand loved his wife and set out barefoot on the holy trek. But along the road, he met an honest basket-weaver who knew the priest's scandalous reputation. Suspecting treachery, the basket-weaver packed Hildebrand inside a large willow hamper and carried him back into his own village cottage on the pretext of seeking shelter.

Through the wicker slats, Hildebrand watched the table laden with roasted birds, fine pies, and flagons of wine. The priest and the unfaithful wife feasted merrily, singing mocking verses about the foolish husband wandering barefoot through the briars.

When the priest boastfully sang, "Would that I could sing like a bird in the hedgerow!" Hildebrand burst out of the basket with his stout oak walking staff in hand. "Here is the bird you asked to hear!" cried Hildebrand.

He dealt the thieving priest such a thorough thrashing that the scoundrel leaped through the open window into the bramble ditch, and sent his ungrateful wife packing back to her parents, sitting down at his own table to enjoy the roasted capon in solitary peace.
moral: Deception and betrayal within the home are swiftly exposed when wit confronts foolishness.

title: The Three Little Birds variant

full_text:
Three sisters were tending sheep near the royal meadows when the king rode by. The eldest said, "If I marry the king, I will spin him the finest shirts." The second said, "If I marry the king, I will bake him bread sweeter than honey." But the youngest whispered, "If I marry the king, I will bear him three golden-haired children who weep pearls and laugh roses."

The king chose the youngest sister and married her in great joy. But her envious older sisters conspired with the wicked queen-mother. Whenever the young queen gave birth—first to two brave boys and then to a lovely girl, each with a golden star upon their brows—the sisters stole the babies away, threw them into the rushing river, and placed whimpering puppies in their cradles, driving the king to banish his heartbroken wife to a stone tower.

Providence watched over the children. A kindly fisherman drew them from the water in his net, raised them as his own, and taught them gentle manners. When the siblings grew up, they journeyed to find the magical singing bird, the golden water, and the dancing tree that could restore their royal heritage.

Guided by their pure hearts, the siblings broke the mountain enchantment and captured the miraculous speaking bird. Brought before the king at a great royal banquet, the bird sang the true tale of the discarded babies, the wicked aunt's deceit, and the innocent queen weeping in her tower.

Overwhelmed with remorse and joy, the king embraced his three golden-starred children, released his faithful queen from her tower, and banished the envious sisters forever, filling the royal realm with long-lost laughter and song.
moral: Innocent children protected by providence cannot be destroyed by wicked slander.

title: The Water of Life (Das Wasser des Lebens)
summary: An old king lay grievously ill, and physicians announced that only the Water of Life from an enchanted castle could restore his failing pulse. His two older sons rode out in turn,...
keywords: the water of life (das wasser des lebens)
full_text:
An old king lay grievously ill, and physicians announced that only the Water of Life from an enchanted castle could restore his failing pulse. His two older sons rode out in turn, puffed up with pride, dreaming only of securing the crown for themselves. Along the trail, each encountered a small dwarf who asked where they were galloping; the haughty princes insulted the dwarf and were consequently led into narrow mountain gorges where their horses could neither advance nor turn back, trapping them in stone canyons.

The youngest prince, riding solely out of pure love for his ailing father, set out next. When he met the little dwarf, he greeted him respectfully and explained his filial quest. The grateful dwarf gave him an iron wand to strike the castle gates three times and two loaves of bread to feed the ravenous lions guarding the inner courtyard. "Enter at the stroke of twelve," warned the dwarf, "and make haste to leave before the clock strikes twelve-and-one, or the gates will shut forever."

The youngest prince pacified the lions, entered the luminous palace, and found an enchanted sleeping princess. She rejoiced at her release, promised to marry him in a year, and told him to draw the Water of Life from the fountain. Escaping just as the clock struck one, the prince rode back with the flask.

Along the road, he used his magical bread and staff to rescue three kingdoms from famine and war, and compassionately secured the release of his imprisoned brothers. But the treacherous older brothers secretly stole the Water of Life while the youngest slept, substituting bitter salt sea-water in his flask. A year later, the princess laid a road of pure gold before her palace gates, commanding that whoever rode straight down the middle was her true groom. The older brothers, afraid of scratching the gold, rode to the sides and were turned away. The youngest prince, thinking only of his beloved bride, galloped straight over the golden pavement. The joyous princess welcomed him, the old king learned of the treachery, and the humble prince was crowned in honor and everlasting peace.

title: Doctor Knowall (Doktor Allwissend)
summary: A poor peasant named Fish hauled a load of two cords of firewood into town with his two oxen and sold them to a wealthy physician for two talers. While receiving his pay, Fish saw...
full_text:
A poor peasant named Fish hauled a load of two cords of firewood into town with his two oxen and sold them to a wealthy physician for two talers. While receiving his pay, Fish saw the doctor dining on roast fowl and delicate pastries in a luxurious velvet coat. The peasant sighed, "Ah, how wonderful it must be to be a doctor and live so grandly! Could a poor man like me ever become one?"

"Easily enough," laughed the doctor. "Sell your oxen and wagon, buy an ABC book with a picture of a rooster on the cover, purchase a fine coat and spectacles, and paint a sign over your cottage door saying: I am Doctor Knowall."

Fish followed the counsel precisely. Soon, a wealthy nobleman whose treasury of golden coins had been stolen arrived at his door, begging Doctor Knowall to find his lost gold. Fish agreed on one condition: his good wife Grete must sit at the grand feast beside him.

At the nobleman's manor, four servants who had actually stolen the money served dinner. When the first servant brought the first dish, Fish nudged his wife, saying, "Grete, that is the first!"—meaning the first course. The terrified servant, convinced his guilt had been exposed, whispered to his fellow thieves that the Doctor knew everything.

When the second and third servants brought their dishes, Fish exclaimed, "That is the second!" and "That is the third!" driving the thieves to trembling panic. During the fourth course, the nobleman asked the Doctor to guess what lay hidden beneath a covered silver bowl. Fish looked at the closed dish, panicked, and whispered mournfully to himself, "Alas, poor Fish, you are caught!" Under the lid was a cooked fish. The nobleman gasped in admiration.

The terrified servants cornered Doctor Knowall in the corridor, confessed their crime, and gave him the secret location of the stolen gold in exchange for keeping their names secret. Fish led the nobleman to the hiding spot, was rewarded with a mountain of gold, and became celebrated far and wide as the greatest sage in the land.
moral: A calm demeanor and a stroke of lucky wit can turn an ordinary soul into an undisputed sage.

title: The Spirit in the Glass Bottle (Der Geist im Glas)

full_text:
A poor woodcutter worked from morning till evening to save enough money to send his only son to school. The lad was clever and learned diligently, but before he could complete his studies, his father's meager savings ran out, and the youth returned home to chop timber in the forest.

One afternoon, while resting beneath a colossal ancient oak tree, the boy heard a muffled, trembling voice calling from beneath the roots: "Let me out! Let me out!" Digging into the moss, he uncovered a sealed glass flagon. He uncorked the bottle, and instantly a thick column of dark smoke poured out, condensing into a gigantic, terrifying spirit that towered over the trees.

"I am Mercurius!" roared the demon. "I have been locked in this bottle for centuries, and my reward to whoever releases me is to snap his neck!"

The lad did not tremble. With supreme composure, he smiled and said, "Before I let you snap my neck, prove to me that you truly came from that tiny flagon! A titan of your vast stature could never have fit inside."

"You doubt my greatness?" roared the vain spirit. Shrinking himself into a thin vapor, the demon poured himself entirely back into the bottle to demonstrate his power. In a flash, the boy jammed the cork tightly back into the neck, trapping the spirit once again.

Realizing he had been outsmarted, the spirit begged for mercy, promising the boy an enchanted rag that could heal any wound and turn plain iron into pure silver. The boy accepted the treasure and freed the spirit. With the magical cloth, the youth turned his rusty axe into silver, paid for his medical studies, and became the most renowned physician in the realm, celebrated for both his brilliant mind and his miraculous healing touch.
moral: Sharp intellect and presence of mind can outwit ancient magic and turn peril into lasting prosperity.

title: The Devil's Sooty Brother
summary: A discharged soldier who received neither pension nor work wandered hungry through a desolate heath until he met a mysterious stranger clad in green who offered him employment. The...
full_text:
A discharged soldier who received neither pension nor work wandered hungry through a desolate heath until he met a mysterious stranger clad in green who offered him employment. The task was simple: the soldier was to tend the roaring fires beneath the cauldrons in the nether halls, sweep the ash, and never peer under the lids. For seven years, he was forbidden from washing his face, combing his hair, or clipping his nails.

The soldier kept his contract faithfully. He swept the soot, shoveled coal, and resisted all temptations. Once, curiosity tempted him to lift a cauldron lid, and he saw his old tyrannical military officers stewing inside, but he promptly replaced the cover and added more fuel.

When the seven years concluded, the master praised the soldier's unwavering discipline. He filled the soldier's knapsack with sweepings of soot, which transformed into glistening nuggets of pure gold the moment he reached the upper world, and gave him a magical flute.

Returning home unwashed and coated in thick black soot, the soldier looked like a fearsome monster. At the village inn, the innkeeper mocked him and tried to rob him. But the soldier called upon his nether acquaintances to terrify the thief, cleaned his face with sweet mountain spring water, and revealed a handsome, noble warrior. Clad in golden armor, he won the hand of a gracious princess and lived in honored wealth, having earned his fortune through fearless endurance and unwavering obedience to his word.
moral: Faithful service without meddling curiosity yields rich rewards and silences scorn.

title: The Bearskin variant
summary: A brave soldier was discharged with nothing but a crust of bread and three bullets. In his despair, he struck a bargain with a mysterious shadowy wanderer in the deep pine woods: t...
full_text:
A brave soldier was discharged with nothing but a crust of bread and three bullets. In his despair, he struck a bargain with a mysterious shadowy wanderer in the deep pine woods: the soldier was to wear a heavy bearskin cloak for seven years, never washing, combing his hair, or trimming his nails. In exchange, the pockets of his coat would remain inexhaustibly filled with gold coins. If he died within the seven years, his soul was forfeit; if he survived, he would be rich and free forever.

For years, the soldier wandered the world as 'Bearskin.' Wherever he went, he gave immense sums of gold to the poor, asking only that they pray for his endurance. People recoiled from his terrifying appearance, but his boundless charity won him quiet blessings across the kingdom.

In the sixth year, Bearskin arrived at an inn where an honest merchant sat weeping, having lost all his goods and facing a debtor's prison. Bearskin paid all the merchant's debts. In gratitude, the merchant offered him one of his three daughters in marriage. The two elder daughters mocked Bearskin's hideous fur and soot-covered face, declaring they would rather marry a wild beast. But the youngest daughter, seeing his kind eyes and gentle voice, accepted him, saying, "He has saved my father, and I will be faithful to him."

Bearskin broke a gold ring in half, gave her one piece, and kept the other, promising to return when his seven years were fulfilled.

When the final hour struck, Bearskin bathed in clear mountain waters, combed his golden hair, trimmed his beard, and donned a magnificent velvet suit. He rode to the merchant's manor in a regal carriage. The older sisters courted the handsome nobleman eagerly, but Bearskin approached the youngest daughter, dropped his half of the gold ring into her wineglass, and embraced his faithful bride, who had loved him when the world saw only a monster.
moral: True nobility of heart sees through ragged appearances to love the steadfast soul beneath.

title: The Willow Wren and the Bear
summary: One sunny afternoon, the Bear and the Wolf were walking in the forest when they heard a bird singing with angelic beauty from a thicket of hazel bushes. The Bear stopped and asked,...
keywords: the willow wren and the bear
full_text:
One sunny afternoon, the Bear and the Wolf were walking in the forest when they heard a bird singing with angelic beauty from a thicket of hazel bushes. The Bear stopped and asked, "Brother Wolf, what magnificent creature sings so sweetly?"

"That is the king of birds," replied the Wolf. "We must bow before him."

The Bear, curious to see the royal palace, waited until the Willow-Wren and his queen flew off to gather worms. He crept up to the nest and peered in, seeing five tiny, naked chicks shivering in the moss. "Is this a palace?" growled the Bear with contempt. "These are not royal children; they are filthy, wretched little runts!"

When the parent wrens returned, the little chicks chirped in outraged sorrow, refusing to eat a single gnat until the Bear was punished for insulting royal blood. The King-Wren flew straight to the Bear's den and formally declared war: a battle of all creatures of the air against all beasts of the forest.

The Bear summoned lions, oxen, stags, wolves, and boars. The Wren summoned eagles, owls, hornets, bees, gnats, and flies. The Wren sent the Mosquito as a spy to discover the enemy's signals. The Fox had been appointed general of the four-legged beasts, using his bushy tail as a flag: held high meant attack, dropped low meant retreat.

When the battle began, the Wren commanded a squadron of hornets to sting the Fox directly under his tail with all their might. The agony was so intense that the Fox could not hold his tail up; he clamped it between his legs and fled yelping toward the river. Seeing their general's flag down, the lions, bears, and wolves panicked and scattered in wild retreat.

The King-Wren then flew to the Bear's cave and demanded an apology. The humiliated Bear was forced to kneel before the tiny nest and beg the chicks for forgiveness, proving that arrogance toward the small brings ruinous disgrace.
moral: Never insult the small and humble; clever strategy and united allies defeat lumbering brute strength.

title: The Sweet Porridge (Sweet Soup)
summary: Once upon a time, there lived a poor, pious little girl and her widowed mother at the edge of a village. They were so impoverished that they had not even a crust of stale bread lef...
full_text:
Once upon a time, there lived a poor, pious little girl and her widowed mother at the edge of a village. They were so impoverished that they had not even a crust of stale bread left in the cupboard. Weeping with hunger, the girl walked into the forest, where an ancient, kindly woman took pity on her.

The old woman gave her a small iron cooking pot and instructed: "Whenever you say, 'Cook, little pot, cook,' it will boil sweet, rich porridge. When you say, 'Stop, little pot, stop,' it will cease cooking."

The girl brought the pot home, and she and her mother enjoyed sweet, delicious porridge every day, banishing their hunger forever.

One morning, while the girl was out walking, the mother felt hungry and said, "Cook, little pot, cook!" The pot began bubbling with fragrant, sweet porridge. The mother ate until she was satisfied, but when she wished the pot to cease, she forgot the magic words! She said, "No more, little pot!" and "That is enough!" but the pot kept boiling.

Porridge poured over the rim, filled the kitchen, covered the parlor, surged out into the street, and flowed into neighboring cottages as if it meant to feed the entire universe! The terrified villagers climbed upon their roofs as sweet porridge flooded the lane.

At last, the little girl returned home. Seeing the sweet river, she called out clearly, "Stop, little pot, stop!" The pot instantly ceased boiling. But whoever wished to enter the village for the next three days was obliged to eat his way through a street of sweet porridge!
moral: Blessings bring abundant nourishment, but carelessness with instructions leads to overflowing chaos.

title: Wise Folks
summary: A country peasant named Hans bought a fat cow at the fair, but being simple of mind, he traded it for a goat, the goat for a sheep, the sheep for a goose, the goose for a hen, and...
full_text:
A country peasant named Hans bought a fat cow at the fair, but being simple of mind, he traded it for a goat, the goat for a sheep, the sheep for a goose, the goose for a hen, and finally the hen for a bag of rotten apples. When he reached home, his wife praised his wonderful trades and kissed him affectionately, thrilled that they had apples to bake.

Seeing this astonishing scene, a traveling gentleman made a wager with Hans: "If your wife did not scold you for losing a cow for rotten apples, I will wager a bag of gold that the next woman in the village is equally foolish!"

They tested the neighbor woman, Dame Christine. Hans told her that a wanderer from heaven had arrived in the village asking for warm coats and gold to give to her deceased first husband, who was walking around paradise shivering in rags.

The credulous woman immediately packed her second husband's best wool coat, fine leather boots, and all his silver thalers into a bundle and handed them to the traveler, begging him to deliver them to her departed spouse.

When her second husband returned from the fields and heard of the folly, he leaped on his fastest horse to pursue the thief. But Hans sat by the roadside, pointed toward the clouds, and told the rider that the celestial messenger had flown straight into the blue sky on a golden chariot. The husband dismounted, left his horse, and climbed a tall pine tree to search the clouds, while Hans led the horse away, laughing heartily at how easily wise folks lose their senses when superstition takes the reins.
moral: Gullibility invites mockery, while honest wit laughs at human pretension.

title: Tales of the Paddock
summary: A sweet, innocent little country child would sit every afternoon on the stone terrace behind her mother's cottage, eating a wooden bowl of sweet milk and crumbled white bread. When...
full_text:
A sweet, innocent little country child would sit every afternoon on the stone terrace behind her mother's cottage, eating a wooden bowl of sweet milk and crumbled white bread. Whenever she sat down, a little spotted toad would hop out from the foundation stones to share her meal.

The child loved the creature dearly and would tap her wooden spoon upon the grass, singing: "Little toad, hop out to me, come and drink your milk with glee!" The toad would lap the warm milk from her spoon, and the child grew rosy and happy in its company.

Once, when the toad ate only the milk and left the bread, the little girl gently tapped its head with her spoon, scolding softly: "Eat breadcrumbs too, little thing, not just the cream!" The toad obeyed like a gentle pet.

When the anxious mother saw the creature one day, she took fright and struck the toad dead with a broom. Immediately, the little child grew pale and sad; she lost her joyful smile, refused her meals, and soon faded away like a wilting flower, illustrating how the delicate bonds of innocent love are woven into the very fabric of life.

title: The Poor Miller's Boy and the Cat

full_text:
An aging miller who had no children announced to his three apprentices that whoever brought him the finest horse should inherit the mill, while the others must seek their fortunes elsewhere. The two older apprentices were clever and boastful, while the youngest, Hans, was considered simple and mocked by everyone.

The apprentices set out into the world. In the woods, the older two abandoned Hans to wander alone. Hans reached an enchanted clearing where he met a small, elegant tabby cat who asked him where he was going. Hans explained his quest for a horse. "Serve me faithfully for seven years," said the cat, "and I will give you the most magnificent steed on earth."

Hans agreed. He chopped wood with silver axes, carried water in silver pails, and swept the cat's castle, where twelve kittens served as courtiers. Hans never complained, working with gentle loyalty day after day.

When seven years ended, the cat led Hans to the forest edge and told him to go home; the horse would follow in due time. Hans returned to the mill in rags. His former companions laughed, showing off two lame, half-blind nags they had purchased, and refused Hans shelter in the house, forcing him to sleep in the goose-pen.

The next morning, a dazzling carriage drawn by six magnificent silver stallions rolled into the mill yard, carrying an exquisitely beautiful princess. Stepping down, she revealed herself as the enchanted cat Hans had served so loyally. She presented the old miller with a magnificent horse, gave Hans the grandest estate in the kingdom, and wed the faithful youth in radiant splendor.
moral: The humble and faithful servant receives blessings beyond the dreams of boastful schemers.

title: The Two Travelers

full_text:
Two travelers journeyed together: an honest, good-natured tailor with a cheerful heart, and a bitter, malicious shoemaker whose soul was dark with envy. When they crossed a desolate, trackless forest, food ran out. The cruel shoemaker refused to share his bread with the starving tailor unless the tailor allowed him to put out one of his eyes. Driven by desperate hunger, the tailor consented.

A few days later, starving once more, the shoemaker demanded the tailor's other eye before giving him another crust. Blinded and helpless, the tailor was abandoned beneath a gallows outside a strange town.

As night fell, two ravens perched upon the gallows spoke in human speech: "If only mortals knew that the morning dew falling upon the moss beneath this tree can restore sight to the blind!" The tailor rubbed the fresh morning dew upon his eyelids, and instantly his vision returned, clearer and sharper than ever.

Entering the city, the tailor used his kindness and skill to help wild beasts—saving storks, ants, and bees from peril. When the king announced impossible tasks to build a royal palace in a single night and find a water spring in the desert, the grateful beasts came to the tailor's aid, completing every task in marvel. The overjoyed king gave him his daughter's hand and made him royal counselor.

The wicked shoemaker, hearing of the tailor's incredible fortune, rushed to the gallows hoping to overhear secrets of wealth. But the ravens mistook him for a thief and pecked out his eyes. Stumbling blindly into the desert, he perished in misery, reaping the bitter harvest of his own cruelty.
moral: Malice and cruelty lead to blindness and ruin, while innocent virtue is restored and exalted.

title: Hans My Hedgehog (Hans mein Igel)
summary: A country peasant, mocked by neighbors for having no children, cried in frustration, "I will have a child, even if it is a hedgehog!" His wife soon gave birth to a boy whose upper...
full_text:
A country peasant, mocked by neighbors for having no children, cried in frustration, "I will have a child, even if it is a hedgehog!" His wife soon gave birth to a boy whose upper body was covered in sharp hedgehog quills. They named him Hans My Hedgehog.

Hans lived behind the stove for eight years, neglected and shunned. Finally, he asked his father for a bagpipe, saddled his rooster, and rode out into the deep woods, where he perched upon a tall pine tree, playing music so enchantingly that the wild forest creatures stopped to listen.

Two different kings, lost in the woods on separate occasions, heard Hans's music and asked for guidance back to their realms. To each, Hans promised a safe path home on one condition: they must pledge in writing that whatever first met them at the castle gates should belong to Hans.

The first king, dishonest and proud, wrote a false promise, thinking a hedgehog could not read. When he arrived home, his daughter ran out to embrace him. When Hans arrived to claim her, the princess mocked his quills. Hans pricked her pride, tore her fine gown with his bristles, and left her in disgrace.

The second king kept his word faithfully. When his loving daughter ran to meet him, she embraced the hedgehog with sweet grace, honoring her father's oath. Hans placed his spiky skin beside the hearth on their wedding night; the loyal guards cast the hedgehog hide into the fire, breaking the ancient enchantment. Hans emerged as a handsome, noble prince of breathtaking beauty, ruling the kingdom in peace and honor.
moral: Keeping a sacred promise brings honor and transformation, while breaking faith brings sorrow.

title: The Shroud
summary: A devoted mother had a little seven-year-old boy who was so sweet, bright, and obedient that everyone who looked upon him loved him. Suddenly, the child fell ill and died, breaking...
full_text:
A devoted mother had a little seven-year-old boy who was so sweet, bright, and obedient that everyone who looked upon him loved him. Suddenly, the child fell ill and died, breaking his mother's heart into a thousand pieces.

Day and night, the grief-stricken mother wept bitter tears, refusing all food, sleep, or comfort. In her agony, she watered the grave with ceaseless lamentations.

One night, the little boy appeared before her in his white burial shroud, with glowing eyes and the gentle halo of a departed angel. He carried a small earthen vessel and stood softly by the foot of her bed.

"Dear mother," whispered the child, "I beg you, cease your weeping! Look at my burial shroud: your endless tears fall upon it without stopping, soaking it through with heavy dampness, so that I cannot rest peacefully in my little bed."

The mother's heart was pierced with tender compassion. She dried her tears, swallowed her bitter grief, and placed her sorrow in peaceful acceptance. The following night, the little boy appeared once more, smiling radiantly, holding a tiny candle whose light illuminated the room. "Look, dear mother," he smiled, "my shroud is dry now, and I can sleep in sweet, eternal peace." The mother bowed her head in serene comfort, knowing love endures beyond the grave.
moral: Excessive weeping disturbs the resting soul; gentle acceptance brings peace to the living and the departed.

title: The Jew Among Thorns
summary: An honest servant worked faithfully for three years for a skinflint master, who at the end of the term handed him a meager pittance of three copper farthings. The cheerful lad took...
full_text:
An honest servant worked faithfully for three years for a skinflint master, who at the end of the term handed him a meager pittance of three copper farthings. The cheerful lad took the small coins without anger, praising the master and heading singing down the highway.

In the forest, he met an elderly wanderer who begged for alms. The generous youth gave away all three copper coins without hesitation. In gratitude, the wanderer granted him three wishes: a magical crossbow that never missed its mark, a fiddle that forced anyone hearing it to dance, and the power that no one could refuse his first request.

Further along the path, he met an avaricious, dishonest merchant who stood gazing covetously at a singing thrush perched high in a thick briar bush. The youth shot the bird with his bow, and it fell into the center of the dense thorn hedge. When the greedy merchant scrambled in to grab it, the youth began playing his magic fiddle.

Instantly, the merchant was compelled to dance wildly, leaping and hopping among the sharp thorns, tearing his coat and crying for mercy. He begged the youth to stop, tossing him a bag of gold coins before being released.

Furious at his humiliation, the merchant ran to the judge, falsely accusing the boy of being a violent highway robber who had beaten him and stolen his gold. The youth was dragged to the gallows. Before the rope was tightened, the boy made his final request: to play one last tune upon his violin.

As the first lively notes rang out, the judge, the executioner, the bailiffs, the horses, and the deceitful merchant all burst into an uncontrollable, frantic jig, dancing in circles until they were completely exhausted. The judge begged him to cease, promising him total pardon. The terrified merchant confessed his slanderous lies, and the merry lad walked free with honor and joy.
moral: Generosity and cheerfulness gain magical aid, while greed and false accusations fall into their own traps.

title: The Skillful Huntsman
summary: A young huntsman, having mastered his craft, set out into the world. In a desolate moor, he encountered three colossal giants roasting an ox around a roaring bonfire. By firing his...
full_text:
A young huntsman, having mastered his craft, set out into the world. In a desolate moor, he encountered three colossal giants roasting an ox around a roaring bonfire. By firing his arrows from the dark pine boughs, he knocked away their morsels until they surrendered, begging him to become their sharpshooter to help them capture a nearby fortress.

The clever huntsman led the giants to the fortress, but instead of helping them conquer it, he tricked them into a deep pit and slew the wicked brutes, saving the sleeping castle.

Entering the silent royal palace, he found a princess sleeping peacefully, unaware of the danger. He carved off the three giants' tongues as proof of his deed, cut a piece of the princess's embroidered gown, and took her golden ring before walking away into the night without seeking empty praise.

The royal captain of the guard found the dead giants next morning. He severed their heads, brought them before the king, and claimed the glory, demanding the princess's hand. The terrified princess, knowing the captain was a cowardly boaster, delayed the wedding for a year.

On the eve of the royal wedding, the true huntsman arrived at the town inn. He sent an obedient hound to the palace, which retrieved bread from the king's table and wine from the royal cellar. Astonished, the king summoned the hunter.

The huntsman laid the giants' tongues, the embroidered fabric, and the princess's golden ring upon the table. The overjoyed princess recognized her true savior, the cowardly captain was condemned, and the modest huntsman married the princess in magnificent celebration.
moral: Quiet competence and steadfast valor expose the loud boasts of impostors.

title: The Flail from Heaven
summary: A country peasant drove two oxen to plow his field, but the horn of one ox grew so immense that it reached straight toward the sky. When the peasant could not turn the plow, he cli...
full_text:
A country peasant drove two oxen to plow his field, but the horn of one ox grew so immense that it reached straight toward the sky. When the peasant could not turn the plow, he climbed up the horn and found himself walking among the clouds.

Up in the celestial heights, he saw threshers beating grain with silver flails. In the excitement of the sight, he knocked a golden flail from the sky, which plummeted back down to the earth and stuck deep into the rocky ground.

To climb down, the peasant gathered chaff and spun it into a long rope. But the rope ended far above the ground. He slid down to the very knot, hanging between heaven and earth. In his pocket, he found a small awl, cut the rope above his head, tied the cut piece below, and leaped down into the middle of a muddy pond, sinking up to his neck.

Unable to climb out of the mire, he calmly hurried home, fetched a spade from his tool shed, and dug himself out of the mud, returning home to his cottage to enjoy a pipe by the hearth, thoroughly satisfied with his grand morning excursion among the clouds.
moral: Tall tales and boundless imagination celebrate the joyful absurdity of human storytelling.

A young prince fell into the clutches of a wicked enchanter-king who demanded three impossible tasks: to cut down a vast forest with an axe of glass, to drain a deep lake with a leaky sieve, and to build a mountain castle in a single night.

The enchanter's daughter, a beautiful princess who loved the prince, used her magical knowledge to complete the tasks for him, shattering the enchanter's power. Realizing her father planned their destruction, she and the prince fled on two swift horses.

When the enchanter pursued them, the princess transformed the horses into a rosebush, a church, and a lake, baffling the pursuers until the enchanter gave up in despair.

Reaching his homeland, the prince went to the palace to prepare for the bridal entry, but his mother kissed him, breaking the sacred spell and causing him to forget his bride entirely.

The abandoned princess lived in a humble cottage near the city. When the prince's wedding to another bride was arranged, the faithful princess obtained permission to dance at the feast. She released two golden doves that pecked at each other, murmuring words of their shared trials on the glass mountain.

The golden words pierced the prince's clouded memory. He recognized his true savior, embraced her with joyful tears, and celebrated his real wedding, casting off oblivion forever in the arms of his devoted bride.
moral: True devotion overcomes mountains of glass, forgets nothing, and breaks the spells of oblivion.
