A haughty princess who considered herself the cleverest soul in the kingdom announced that she would marry whichever suitor could solve her three riddles. Two proud, learned masters arrived with thick books, followed by a diminutive, cheerful tailor who brought only his nimble wit.

The princess asked her riddles, which the learned masters answered with pedantic foolishness, failing utterly. The tailor answered each riddle with sparkling common sense and delightful wit, unraveling every knot the princess tied.

Reluctant to marry a humble tailor, the princess set one final trial: the suitor must spend the night in the royal stable with a ferocious, man-eating brown bear.

The two masters fled in terror, but the little tailor stepped boldly into the stable. When the bear growled and charged with outstretched claws, the tailor calmly took walnuts from his pocket, cracked them between his teeth, and offered some to the beast. The bear tried to crack them, but the tailor had handed him smooth river pebbles. While the bear chewed futilely on stones, the tailor offered to teach him to play the fiddle, securing the bear's paws in a wooden vice on the pretext of trimming his claws.

The tailor then curled up on a pile of sweet hay and slept soundly until morning. When the princess opened the doors, expecting to find bones, she saw the tailor merrily whistling while the trapped bear nodded to the tune. Admitting defeat to his superior wit, the princess married the clever little tailor, and they lived in merry prosperity.
moral: Resourceful ingenuity and a merry heart triumph where physical strength admits defeat.

full_text:
A wandering tailor's apprentice had spent his last farthing and was trudging down a deserted highway when he met an honest old Jew carrying a heavy pack of goods. Driven by desperate greed, the youth struck the traveler down, demanding his money.

As the old man lay dying upon the dusty road, he pointed with a trembling finger toward the morning sun rising over the hills, whispering his final words: "The bright sun will bring it to light!"

The apprentice scoffed, took the meager bag of copper coins, and fled. Years passed, and the crime remained buried. The tailor married, prospered, and became a respected master in a flourishing town, surrounded by loving children and honored by his neighbors.

One bright morning, as he sat at the breakfast table drinking hot coffee, the morning sun shone brightly through the windowpane, casting shimmering reflections across the foam in his cup. The master smiled absentmindedly and muttered aloud, "It would bring it to light, indeed! How absurd!"

His wife asked what he meant by such curious words. Feeling completely secure after so many years, the man foolishly confessed the murder he had committed in his youth, laughing at the dying man's warning.

Horrified by the dark truth, the wife reported the confession to the magistrates. The master was arrested, confessed before the court, and paid the penalty for his ancient crime, proving that though justice may tarry, the bright sun of truth inevitably illuminates every shadow.
moral: No crime remains hidden forever; the light of truth exposes the darkest deeds.

A brave old soldier who had served the king through countless bloody campaigns was discharged without pension or food when peace arrived. Wandering through the wilderness, he sought shelter in the cottage of an old witch.

The witch promised him bread and lodging if he would climb down into a deep, dried-up well and retrieve a small lamp that glowed with an eerie blue light. The soldier climbed down, secured the lamp, but when the witch demanded he hand it up before pulling him out, the wise soldier refused, knowing she meant to leave him to starve. Furious, the witch let go of the rope, dropping him to the muddy bottom.

In the darkness, the soldier took out his pipe and lit it with the blue flame. Instantly, a tiny black dwarf appeared, bowing low and saying, "Master, what is your command? I am the servant of the Blue Light, bound to obey whoever strikes its flame."

The soldier commanded the dwarf to carry him from the well and punish the witch. He then had the dwarf bring the ungrateful king's daughter to his room every midnight to sweep the floor and polish his muddy boots, paying her back for her father's neglect of his soldiers.

When the king discovered the truth, he sent soldiers to execute the veteran. Standing before the gallows, the soldier asked to smoke one final pipe. He struck the Blue Light, summoning an army of spirit warriors that routed the royal guard. The humbled king was forced to surrender his crown to the faithful old soldier, who ruled the kingdom with wisdom, honoring every honest laborer and veteran in the land.
moral: Those who mistreat faithful servants will see justice turn the tables through magical retribution.

There was once a stubborn, wilful child who refused to obey his mother in anything. Whatever she told him to do, he did the opposite, stamping his feet in obstinate defiance and spurning all gentle instruction.

The child fell ill and died, but even in the grave, his stubbornness would not rest. Whenever his little arm was buried beneath the earth, it thrust itself upward through the soil into the open air, refusing to remain peaceful.

The heartbroken mother came to the churchyard, carrying a birch twig. She gently tapped the little hand that reached through the earth, speaking words of maternal discipline and love.

At that loving touch of guidance, the little arm withdrew beneath the soft sod, resting quietly at last beneath the sheltering soil, teaching that the heart finds true peace only when defiance yields to gentle discipline and love.
moral: Stubborn defiance of parental wisdom disturbs the peace of the soul until humility is restored.

full_text:
A holy hermit lived in a lonely mountain cave, spending his days in fasting and prayer. Over the years, pride crept into his heart, until he believed himself purer and more righteous than all other mortals.

One day, he saw a criminal being led to the gallows and muttered in self-righteous contempt, "That wicked sinner deserves nothing but eternal destruction!"

That very night, an angel appeared to the hermit, handing him a dry, withered branch with three brittle twigs. "Take this dead wood," the angel commanded. "Carry it through the world, begging bread from door to door, and never sleep in a bed until three green leaves sprout from these dry twigs. By your harsh judgment, you closed your heart to divine mercy."

The hermit wept in bitter repentance. For decades, he wandered barefoot through storms and heat, sleeping on bare stones, asking for nothing but dry crusts, and comforting the sick and forgotten.

In his extreme old age, he gave his last crust of bread to a starving beggar and knelt beneath an ancient mountain pine to breathe his last prayer of humble remorse. When the morning sun shone upon his peaceful face, three radiant, emerald-green leaves had sprouted from the dry twigs, showing that a truly contrite heart is restored to grace by boundless love.
moral: Divine mercy is broader than human judgment; repentance sprouts green leaves from dry wood.

full_text:
A poor peasant was driving a heavy wagon loaded with casks of wine down a steep, rocky hill when the wagon wheels sank deep into a muddy rut, threatening to overturn the precious cargo. The peasant pushed and pulled with all his might, but the wheels would not budge.

Just then, a gentle woman clothed in sky-blue robes walked down the pathway, radiating maternal grace. Seeing the peasant's distress, she spoke kindly: "Good man, I am weary and thirsty from my long journey; give me a sip of wine from your cask, and your wagon shall be freed."

"Alas, gracious lady," answered the peasant, "I would gladly give you wine, but I have no cup or glass to draw it with."

The lady picked a delicate white-and-pink bindweed blossom growing along the hedge. The flower was shaped like a tiny goblet. She held it beneath the spigot, and the peasant filled it with rich wine. She drank with gentle gratitude, and instantly the heavy wagon rolled smoothly out of the deep mud onto the dry road.

To this day, the country folk call that delicate morning-glory flower 'Our Lady's Little Glass,' reminding all travelers that simple generosity to wanderers carries a quiet, enduring blessing.
moral: Gentle acts of hospitality toward the weary are blessed in the quiet wonders of nature.

full_text:
An aged mother had two beloved sons who were her entire joy in the twilight of her life. Yet within a single year, both young men were taken by fever, leaving the mother alone in her desolate cottage, weeping inconsolably and wondering why she had been left behind.

In her sorrow, she walked to the village church in the dead of night. Through the stained glass, she saw the sanctuary filled with a multitude of departed souls clad in radiant white garments, kneeling in peaceful prayer.

Looking toward the altar, she saw her two sons standing in celestial joy, holding branches of palm and smiling with serene peace. They turned to her and whispered: "Weep no more, dear mother! We were spared the bitter trials and heavy storms of the earthly road, and now dwell in eternal light. Dry your tears, for your love led us to peace."

The aged mother walked back to her cottage with a heart filled with sweet tranquility. She shed no more bitter tears, lived out her remaining days in quiet works of charity, and departed peacefully in the blessed hope of everlasting reunion.
moral: A mother's enduring love is held safely in celestial keeping beyond the trials of this world.

A poor little peasant boy was sent to church by his mother to attend morning prayers. While gazing at the altar, he saw the carved statue of the child Jesus and thought with simple, innocent love, "How cold and hungry you must look up there alone!"

Every morning, the child brought half of his daily crust of bread and laid it gently before the holy image, saying, "Eat with me, little friend, so you will not go hungry."

One morning, the image came to life, smiled with heavenly warmth, and took the bread, saying: "Because you shared your crust with me in pure love, you are invited to my heavenly wedding feast on Sunday morning."

The little boy returned home and told his mother that he had been invited to a glorious wedding. On Sunday morning, the church bells rang, but the little boy did not rise from his bed. His mother walked to his room and found him lying serenely with folded hands, his face glowing with an angelic smile of everlasting joy, having been welcomed into the celestial feast by the friend he had loved so purely.
moral: The innocent faith of a child is welcomed into the highest halls of divine joy.

In ancient times, when the mother of a holy wanderer walked through the dark forest seeking shelter from a venomous serpent that pursued her through the grass, she looked in vain among the tall pines and rigid oaks for a hiding place. The proud trees held their branches high above the ground, offering no refuge from the creeping peril.

At the forest edge stood a humble hazel bush with dense, green boughs sweeping down to the earth. The bush spread its tender leaves and sheltered the gentle traveler beneath its leafy canopy. The venomous snake coiled near the roots but could not penetrate the protective hazel boughs, slithering away into the dark hollows of the earth.

In gratitude for its quiet sanctuary, the traveler blessed the hazel bush, decreeing that from that day forth, its branches would serve as a natural safeguard against serpents, adders, and dark enchantments.

To this day, country folk in the alpine valleys carry a freshly cut hazel wand when traversing rocky moors and serpent-haunted thickets, remembering that the humblest shrub can offer the greatest sanctuary in the hour of peril.
moral: Even humble boughs that provide shelter to the weary receive enduring blessing and protection.

keywords: the dog and the sparrow variant
full_text:
A loyal sheepdog, having served a stingy shepherd until his teeth wore down, was cast out into the highway to starve. Sitting weepingly in a ditch, he was befriended by a clever sparrow who promised to feed him.

The sparrow flew into a butcher's shop, pecked a sausage from the counter, and dropped it for the dog. He did the same at a bakery, feeding his friend until the hound was full and satisfied. The dog curled up on the sunny road to take a peaceful nap.

A cruel wagoner driving a cart pulled by three horses came rumbling down the lane. The sparrow chirped a warning: "Wagoner, turn aside! My friend is sleeping there; do not crush him!"

The arrogant wagoner cracked his whip and intentionally drove his heavy iron-rimmed wheels over the sleeping dog, killing him instantly. "You have slain my friend!" cried the grief-stricken sparrow. "It shall cost you your horses and your cart!"

The sparrow pecked at the bung-hole of the wagoner's wine cask until all the fine wine drained into the dust. Then the bird perched on the horses' heads, pecking at their eyes. title: The Little Folk's Presents

full_text:
A cheerful tailor and a greedy, hunchbacked goldsmith were traveling together through the Black Forest when they heard enchanting music echoing from a moonlit clearing. Parting the hazel bushes, they saw an assembly of tiny woodland dwarfs dancing merrily around an old man with a long white beard.

The old man motioned for the two travelers to sit. Taking a sharp razor, he shaved their heads and beards clean, and then filled their pockets with worthless black coal from the bonfire, gesturing that they should depart in peace.

The hunchbacked goldsmith grumbled bitterly at carrying filthy coal, but the polite tailor thanked the little folk with a courteous bow. In the morning, when they woke at the inn, both were astonished to find that every single piece of coal in their pockets had turned into heavy, glistening nuggets of pure gold! The tailor was overjoyed, while the goldsmith's greed was inflamed tenfold.

"We must return tonight!" insisted the goldsmith. "I will bring gigantic sacks and fill them with coal, becoming richer than the Emperor!"

The tailor refused to go back, satisfied with his fortune. The greedy goldsmith returned alone, offered his bald head, and stuffed two enormous sacks with coal. But when the morning sun rose, his sacks contained only worthless black soot, his old gold had vanished, and he woke to find a second heavy hump grown upon his chest! He returned home in weeping disgrace, while the contented tailor married his sweetheart and lived in generous prosperity.
moral: A contented heart transforms coal into gold, while greedy envy turns riches into heavy soot.

full_text:
A diminutive tailor with a pocketful of needles and a bold heart walked through the forest, seeking adventure. Suddenly, a colossal giant towered over him, growling: "What are you doing here, you wretched fly? If you cross my path again, I will crush you between my fingers!"

"Quiet your shouting!" replied the tailor boldly. "You may be tall, but I possess strength beyond your reckoning. Let us test our mettle!"

The giant picked up a heavy boulder and squeezed it until water trickled from the stone. The tailor laughed, pulled a soft piece of cheese from his knapsack, and squeezed it until whey ran out. The giant, thinking it was stone, was thoroughly baffled.

Next, the giant threw a rock so high into the air that the eye could barely follow it. The tailor released a live willow-wren from his pocket; the bird soared into the clouds and never returned. "Where did your stone go?" laughed the tailor. "Mine flew straight into the sky and refuses to come back down!"

Finally, the giant invited the tailor to carry an uprooted oak tree. "You take the trunk," said the clever tailor, "and I will carry the heavy branches and crown, which are far larger." The giant hoisted the trunk onto his broad shoulder, while the tailor hopped unnoticed into the leafy branches, whistling merrily while the sweating giant carried both the tree and the tailor all the way to his cave.

Convinced that the tiny tailor was an invincible sorcerer, the terrified giant fled into the mountains, leaving the tailor to enjoy the giant's hoard in peace.
moral: Quick wits and clever bluffing easily overcome towering brute force.

title: The Nail
summary: A prosperous merchant had concluded great business at the annual fair, filling his leather saddlebags with silver coins and golden chains. Anxious to reach home before nightfall, h...
full_text:
A prosperous merchant had concluded great business at the annual fair, filling his leather saddlebags with silver coins and golden chains. Anxious to reach home before nightfall, he saddled his horse and rode out of town.

At the inn stables, the groom warned him: "Sir, your horse's left hind shoe is missing a nail. Let me fetch the blacksmith to secure it."

"No time for delays!" shouted the impatient merchant. "The remaining five nails will hold for the few miles I must travel."

He galloped down the stony road. After an hour, the horse cast the loosened horseshoe completely and began to limp over the sharp flints. A peasant along the way warned him: "Good master, your horse is missing a shoe; stop and have it shod at the forge ahead!"

"Never mind," grunted the stubborn merchant. "We are only two miles from the village; the beast can easily endure that much."

A mile further on, the bare hoof split on a jagged boulder, and the horse stumbled, snapped its foreleg, and fell heavily into the ditch, dying upon the stones.

The merchant was forced to leave his faithful steed dead by the roadside, unbuckle his heavy saddlebags, and trudge on foot through the gathering dark, carrying the crushing weight of gold upon his aching back. Weeping with exhaustion, he muttered to himself: "For want of a nail, the shoe was lost; for want of a shoe, the horse was lost; and for want of a horse, the rider walked in misery!"
moral: A little neglect of small details can lead to the total loss of what is most precious.

title: The Poor Boy in the Grave

full_text:
A poor orphan boy was apprenticed to a cruel, hard-hearted farmer and his equally spiteful wife. From morning till dusk, the child was forced to chop heavy timber, clean stables in the freezing snow, and eat moldy crusts, suffering harsh blows for the slightest accident.

One day, the farmer sent the shivering lad to carry a jar of sweet oil to the cellar. Tripping over an icy stone, the jar shattered on the floor. Fearing the farmer's brutal beating, the boy fled into the orchard and hid beneath a barrel of vinegar. When the farmer discovered him, he beat the orphan mercilessly with an ox-hide whip.

Despairing of any mercy in this earthly life, the child saw a jar marked 'Poison' in the pantry—which the farmer had actually filled with sweet honey to keep it safe from thieves. Wishing only for peaceful sleep, the boy ate the entire jar and lay down in an open grave dug in the quiet churchyard, crossing his hands and waiting to die.

Instead of dying of poison, the sweet honey warmed his chilled body and filled him with peaceful dreams. The village pastor found the sleeping child, took him into his warm parsonage, and heard the full tale of the farmer's cruelty. The magistrates stripped the farmer of his wealth to pay for the boy's education, and the gentle orphan grew into a prosperous, compassionate scholar who dedicated his life to protecting the weak.
moral: Cruelty to the defenseless cries out for justice, and peace awaits the pure in heart.

title: The True Bride

full_text:
A beautiful, sweet maiden lived under the tyranny of a cruel stepmother who imposed impossible tasks upon her: spinning twelve pounds of tangled flax in a single day, emptying a deep pond with a cracked wooden spoon, and building a magnificent marble castle overnight.

Weeping at her trials, the maiden was assisted by an ancient fairy godmother with snowy hair, who touched the flax and stone with a hazel wand, completing every impossible task with effortless magic.

The wicked stepmother, exploring the finished marble castle, slipped from the highest parapet and fell to her death, freeing the maiden forever. The girl lived peacefully in the castle until a handsome prince visited and won her heart with vows of eternal fidelity.

The prince returned to his father's palace to prepare the royal wedding, promising to return within three days. But in the city, an evil sorceress cast an enchantment upon him, making him forget his true bride and betrothing him to an arrogant false princess.

The faithful maiden waited for months in vain. Clad in a simple shepherdess gown, she walked to the capital city. She traded three magnificent magical gowns of spun sunbeams, moonbeams, and starlight for permission to spend three nights in the prince's sleeping chamber.

On the third night, the prince avoided the drugged wine given to him by the false bride. He heard the gentle shepherdess weeping and singing of their marble castle and the impossible spinning tasks. The dark fog of the enchantment lifted from his mind; he recognized his true bride, cast off the false pretender, and married the faithful maiden in glorious joy.
moral: Enduring patience and pure love triumph over the harshest trials of cruelty and deceit.

title: The Hare and the Hedgehog
summary: On a crisp autumn morning, a hedgehog walked through the turnip field, humming a cheerful tune. He met the long-legged Hare, who greeted him with sneering arrogance: "Look at your...
full_text:
On a crisp autumn morning, a hedgehog walked through the turnip field, humming a cheerful tune. He met the long-legged Hare, who greeted him with sneering arrogance: "Look at your crooked, stubby little legs! How can anyone crawl through life with such ridiculous pins?"

"My legs may be short," bristled the hedgehog, "but they can run faster than your long stilts! I will wager a golden thaler and a bottle of fine wine that I can beat you in a race across this plowed field!"

The Hare laughed uproariously and accepted the challenge. The hedgehog hurried home and told his wife: "Dress yourself in a waistcoat like mine and come to the lower end of the furrow. When the Hare arrives, simply stand up and shout: 'I am here already!'"

The race began. The Hare bounded forward like the wind, kicking up dust and leaping over furrows. When he reached the far end, out popped the hedgehog's wife, dusting her prickles and calling: "I am here already!"

Baffled and furious, the Hare turned around and sprinted back: "Run again!" When he touched the top furrow, the hedgehog himself stepped out, smiling: "I am here already!"

Seventy-three times the proud Hare galloped back and forth along the furrows, growing more exhausted and bewildered with every dash, while at every finish line a prickly head popped up with the cheerful cry: "I am here already!"

On the seventy-fourth sprint, the Hare collapsed in the mud, completely spent. The hedgehog took his golden thaler and his bottle of wine, and strolled happily home with his clever wife, teaching everyone that a clever mind and a loyal partner can outrun the fastest boaster in the world.
moral: Arrogant mockery of another’s stature is swiftly humbled by teamwork and clever wits.

title: The Spindle, the Shuttle, and the Needle
summary: A young orphan girl lived in a tiny cottage at the edge of the village, having inherited nothing from her godmother except a spinning spindle, a weaver's shuttle, and an embroidery...
keywords: the spindle, the shuttle, and the needle
full_text:
A young orphan girl lived in a tiny cottage at the edge of the village, having inherited nothing from her godmother except a spinning spindle, a weaver's shuttle, and an embroidery needle. She worked with cheerful diligence from sunrise to sunset, singing sweet songs while flax transformed into shimmering linen under her nimble fingers.

Meanwhile, a king's son traveled through the realm in search of a bride. He declared he would marry neither the richest nor the proudest maiden, but the one who was both the poorest and the most industrious, whose modest heart was rich in virtue.

The prince rode past the mansions of proud noblewomen who flaunted their silks, and finally paused before the orphan's humble cottage. Peeking through the green vines, he saw the maiden spinning with graceful diligence, clothed in simple, spotlessly clean linen. He smiled, rode on, and waited.

The maiden took her magical spindle, set it on the floor, and sang: "Spindle, run after my love, and bring the bridegroom home!" The spindle bounded out the door, trailing a golden thread across the fields straight to the prince's horse.

She took her shuttle and sang: "Shuttle, weave a golden path for my bridegroom!" The shuttle flew through the air, weaving a magnificent carpet of red velvet and golden blossoms extending from the highway to her doorstep.

She took her needle and sang: "Needle, adorn my humble room for my prince!" The needle darted like lightning, covering the walls with green tapestry and dressing the chairs in fine damask.

When the prince followed the golden thread into the cottage, he found the modest maiden waiting in quiet grace. Embracing her, he said, "You are the poorest and the richest; you shall be my royal bride!" He lifted her onto his steed, and they celebrated a wedding whose splendor shone throughout the land.
moral: Diligence, modest virtue, and quiet industry attract true nobility and lifelong honor.

title: The Peasant and the Devil
summary: A crafty peasant had plowed his field until twilight when he saw a mound of glowing embers in the middle of the furrow. Approaching cautiously, he found a black, impish devil sitti...
full_text:
A crafty peasant had plowed his field until twilight when he saw a mound of glowing embers in the middle of the furrow. Approaching cautiously, he found a black, impish devil sitting upon the coals, grinning maliciously.

"Are you sitting upon hidden treasure?" asked the peasant.

"Indeed I am!" replied the devil. "More gold and silver than you have ever seen in all your days! And it shall be yours on one condition: for two years, you must share the harvest of this field with me. What grows above the ground shall belong to me, and what grows beneath the earth shall belong to you."

The peasant agreed with a hearty handshake. When planting time arrived, the clever peasant sowed turnips and carrots. When autumn came, the devil arrived to collect his share, finding only withered yellow leaves and dry weeds, while the peasant dug up great wagons of plump, juicy roots and sweet turnips!

Furious at being outwitted, the devil cried: "Next year the agreement is reversed! What grows beneath the earth belongs to me, and what grows above the ground belongs to you!"

"Agreed," smiled the peasant. The following spring, the peasant sowed wheat and oats. When harvest season returned, the peasant reaped golden grain and heavy sheaves of wheat, while the furious devil was left to dig up useless hairy roots and stubble from the dirt.

Seeing that he could never outsmart the honest peasant's practical agricultural wisdom, the devil screamed in frustration and plunged deep into the fiery depths, leaving the peasant to unearth the colossal chest of gold and silver in complete peace.
moral: A clever and industrious peasant can easily outsmart the greed of sinister schemers.

title: The Crumbs on the Table
summary: A mother bird spoke to her three young offspring perched on the window ledge: "Listen to me, little ones! The mistress of this farmhouse has gone to the garden, and breadcrumbs lie...
full_text:
A mother bird spoke to her three young offspring perched on the window ledge: "Listen to me, little ones! The mistress of this farmhouse has gone to the garden, and breadcrumbs lie scattered upon the parlor table. But beware: stay outside, for cats prowl beneath the chairs, and brooms strike swiftly."

The two older fledglings obeyed their mother's prudent counsel, pecking safely at clover seeds in the sunny orchard.

The youngest fledgling, boastful and reckless, puffed out his feathers: "What do I care for cautious warnings? The table is covered with sweet cake crumbs, and I am far too nimble for any old cat or broom!"

He fluttered through the open window, landed boldly on the mahogany table, and began gorging himself on sweet buttered crumbs.

Suddenly, the kitchen door swung wide. The housemaid swept into the room with a heavy broom, while the ginger cat leaped from behind the curtain. The frightened little bird panicked, flapped against the closed window glass, and was seized in an instant, learning in his final breath that rash disobedience to loving advice leads to swift destruction.
moral: Prudent caution protects against hidden perils; foolish rashness ends in a sudden snare.

title: The Sea-Hare
summary: A haughty princess dwelled in a high castle containing twelve enchanted windows. Looking through the first, she could see every corner of her palace; through the sixth, the entire...
full_text:
A haughty princess dwelled in a high castle containing twelve enchanted windows. Looking through the first, she could see every corner of her palace; through the sixth, the entire kingdom; and through the twelfth, every speck on the surface of the whole earth! She proclaimed that whoever could hide from her for three days should marry her, but anyone she discovered would lose his head upon the city walls.

Ninety-nine boastful suitors had perished when a handsome, humble youth arrived. On his journey, he had spared an eagle caught in a snare, a wounded raven, and a stranded fish gasping on the riverbank.

On the first day, the eagle hid the youth high inside a cloud; the princess looked through the eleventh window, spotted him, and called him down.

On the second day, the fish swam with the youth deep into the ocean depths, hiding him inside an oyster shell; through the twelfth window, the princess detected his presence and summoned him back.

On the third day, the youth sat in despair. A tiny sea-hare—a mystical woodland creature he had saved—ran to him, transformed the youth into an invisible gnat, and hid him beneath the princess's own heavy braided tresses!

The princess looked through all twelve windows in mounting fury, unable to find the suitor anywhere on land, sea, or cloud. When the clock struck noon, the gnat hopped out and resumed his handsome form before her eyes. Humbled by his superior cleverness and charmed by his grace, the princess acknowledged defeat, married the gallant youth, and ruled the kingdom in joyous harmony.
moral: Mercy toward wild creatures earns magical allies that surpass the keenest royal eyes.

title: The Master Thief
summary: A poor peasant was visited by a wealthy gentleman in a luxurious carriage who revealed himself as the peasant's long-lost son. The son admitted that he had become a Master Thief, c...
full_text:
A poor peasant was visited by a wealthy gentleman in a luxurious carriage who revealed himself as the peasant's long-lost son. The son admitted that he had become a Master Thief, capable of stealing anything without shedding blood or breaking iron doors.

The local count, his godfather, tested his skills by setting three impossible challenges: first, to steal the count's favorite horse from the stable guarded by armed sentinels; second, to steal the sheets from the count's bed and the wedding ring from the countess's finger; and third, to steal the priest and sacristan from the village church.

The master thief disguised himself as an old peddler woman, drugged the guards' wine with sleeping draughts, and rode the horse away while the sentinels snored in their saddles.

Next, on a stormy night, he lowered the dummy of a burglar outside the count's window; the count fired his pistol, ran downstairs believing he had killed an intruder, while the thief climbed inside, comforted the trembling countess, asked for the bedsheets to wrap the corpse, and slipped the ring from her finger.

Finally, he appeared in the churchyard dressed as an angel of light with candles fastened to crabs crawling along the grass, announcing the Day of Judgment. The credulous priest and sacristan climbed eagerly into his sack to be carried straight to heaven, only to find themselves dumped into the count's chicken coop!

The amazed count marveled at his godfather's brilliant wit, spared his life, and rewarded him handsomely on condition that he leave the country and use his genius in honorable pursuits.
moral: Ingenious wit can overcome any lock or guard, but true mastery knows when to retire.

full_text:
A brave young drummer walking along the shore of a lake found three delicate pieces of white linen lying on the sand. Pocketing the finest piece, he was visited at midnight by an enchanted maiden who revealed that she was a king's daughter held captive on the Glass Mountain by a cruel witch.

Determined to save her, the drummer marched into the wilderness. He tricked two squabbling giants into surrendering their magical saddle that transported its rider anywhere on earth at a single thought.

Landing atop the Glass Mountain, he confronted the wicked witch. She set him three perilous trials: to chop down an enchanted pine forest with a wooden axe, to clear a swamp with a lead shovel, and to build a golden palace out of bare rocks. The captive princess used her secret magic to complete every task for the brave drummer.

Together, they escaped from the mountain, but on reaching his home village, the drummer kissed his parents, breaking the protective spell and causing him to forget his bride entirely.

When the drummer's wedding to another maiden was arranged, the faithful princess bought her way into his chamber with three magical dresses of sun, moon, and stars. Hearing her sing the words of their Glass Mountain trials, the veil of forgetfulness was torn from his heart. The drummer recognized his true love, dismissed the false match, and wed his devoted princess in unending celebration.
moral: Fearless determination can conquer towering mountains of glass and break the darkest spells.

title: The Ear of Corn
summary: In ancient times, when the earth was young and humanity walked in harmony with nature, stalks of wheat grew five hundred times more abundantly than they do today. Every stalk bore...
full_text:
In ancient times, when the earth was young and humanity walked in harmony with nature, stalks of wheat grew five hundred times more abundantly than they do today. Every stalk bore grains along its entire length, from the root all the way to the tip, providing food in boundless abundance without heavy toil.

One afternoon, a foolish and arrogant woman walked through the village street holding her little child. The child slipped and fell into a muddy puddle, soiling its clothes. Without a thought of gratitude or reverence, the wasteful woman snatched a handful of golden wheat ears from the roadside stalk and used them to wipe the mud from her child's boots.

At that very moment, a voice of divine indignation echoed through the heavens: "Because humanity scorns the sacred bread that nourishes life, no stalk shall ever bear grain again!"

The peasants fell upon their knees in the dust, weeping and begging for mercy, pleading that even if mortals were unworthy, the innocent birds of the air and the beasts of the field must not starve.

Moved by their contrite repentance, the heavens showed mercy: the top of the stalk alone was permitted to bear an ear of grain, while the rest remained bare straw, reminding all generations to treat daily bread with humble gratitude and reverence.
moral: Bread is a sacred gift to be revered; wasteful arrogance brings scarcity and hard toil.

title: The Grave Mound
summary: A wealthy, stingy peasant who had hoarded gold his entire life grew terrified of death. Realizing his worldly wealth could not save his soul, he made a pact with an honest, impover...
full_text:
A wealthy, stingy peasant who had hoarded gold his entire life grew terrified of death. Realizing his worldly wealth could not save his soul, he made a pact with an honest, impoverished neighbor: if the neighbor would guard his grave for three nights after his burial, he would bequeath him half his estate.

The poor neighbor kept his vigil. For the first two nights, cold winds howled through the churchyard, but on the third night, a dark demon appeared, demanding the wealthy miser's soul.

The brave neighbor stood firmly upon the grave mound, drawing a circle with his walking staff and holding his ground. "You cannot have this soul," declared the poor man, "unless you fill my leather riding boot with pure gold pieces!"

The demon flew across the world, gathering hoards of gold to pour into the boot. But the clever neighbor had cut the sole out of the boot and set it over an open cellar grating! As the demon poured gold, it cascaded endlessly into the deep vault.

The demon exhausted his nether treasures trying to fill the bottomless boot until the morning rooster crowed. Scorched by the morning sun, the demon fled into the abyss. The brave neighbor used the immense mountain of gold to relieve the poor, feed the hungry, and build hospitals throughout the province, turning the miser's hoarded curse into a blessing for thousands.
moral: Sharing wealth with the poor protects the soul, and courage in the dark watch defeats the adversary.

title: Old Rinkrank
summary: A king built a sheer Mountain of Glass and announced that whoever could run up to the summit without falling should marry his daughter. The princess herself rode up the slippery gl...
full_text:
A king built a sheer Mountain of Glass and announced that whoever could run up to the summit without falling should marry his daughter. The princess herself rode up the slippery glass on a specially shod horse alongside her favorite suitor. But halfway up, the horse slipped, the mountain cracked open, and the princess plummeted into a deep subterranean cavern.

She found herself imprisoned by an ancient dwarf named Old Rinkrank, who possessed a silver beard so long it dragged across the floor. Rinkrank forced her to cook, wash, and clean his underground palace, while he used an enchanted silver ladder every morning to climb out into the upper world to gather gold.

For years, the princess plotted her escape. One evening, when Rinkrank returned and asked her to wash his long silver beard, she led him to the window and deliberately shut the heavy oak casement onto his beard, pinning him fast to the sill!

Rinkrank screamed and struggled, but the princess refused to release him until he revealed the secret words that opened the mountain and showed her where his ladder was hidden.

Climbing up to the sunlight, she opened the cavern gates, reunited with her joyful prince, and brought down the mountain's riches, while Old Rinkrank was left pinned to his window until he promised never to trap mortals again.
moral: A clever and courageous spirit finds a way out of the deepest underground prisons.

Fearing a similar fate, the youngest son fled into the wide world, learning that an enchanted princess was held captive in the Castle of the Golden Sun, awaiting a hero brave enough to claim the Crystal Ball that held her captor's life.

The youth journeyed across vast wildernesses. Along the way, he resolved a quarrel between two giants who were fighting over a magical cap of invisibility, taking the cap for himself and using its power to slip past the fierce monsters guarding the mountain fortress.

She revealed that the magical Crystal Ball was guarded by a ferocious red bull at the foot of the mountain; inside the bull lay a fiery bird, and inside the bird was a burning egg containing the crystal sphere.

The youth battled the bull. When the fiery bird burst from the beast and took flight, his brother the Eagle soared from the clouds and struck it down. When the burning egg fell into the ocean depths, his brother the Whale surged from the waves and cast the egg onto the shore.

The youth broke the egg, retrieved the sparkling Crystal Ball, and held it before the evil sorcerer. The sorcerer's power crumbled into dust. The youth's brothers were restored to their noble human forms, the princess regained her breathtaking beauty, and the youth wed her in the radiant Castle of the Golden Sun, reigning in joy and peace.
moral: Courage and brotherly devotion can shatter the darkest enchantments and restore beauty.

title: Maid Maleen
summary: Princess Maleen loved a noble prince, but her proud father demanded she marry a wealthy foreign tyrant. When Maleen steadfastly refused to break her vow of love, her furious father...
full_text:
Princess Maleen loved a noble prince, but her proud father demanded she marry a wealthy foreign tyrant. When Maleen steadfastly refused to break her vow of love, her furious father had her walled up inside a dark stone tower with seven years of food and water, along with her loyal waiting maid.

For seven long years, the maidens lived in complete darkness. When their food was exhausted, Maleen used a butter knife to scrape away the mortar between the stones, dislodging a boulder and crawling out into the open sky.

To their horror, the realm had been devastated by enemy armies; the palace was burned, and her father was dead. Maleen and her maid wandered the war-torn lands in rags, finally finding work as scullery maids in the royal kitchen of her beloved prince's court.

Unknown to Maleen, the prince, believing his beloved had perished in the tower, had been pressured into an engagement with an ugly, spiteful foreign princess. The ugly bride, ashamed of her crooked face, forced Maid Maleen to wear the royal bridal gown and walk to the church in her stead, threatening her with death if she revealed the secret.

As Maleen walked down the aisle, she murmured gentle rhymes to a nettle bush, to the churchyard bridge, and to the golden portal, speaking of her true love. The prince marveled at the bride's exquisite beauty and sweet voice, placing a precious golden chain around her neck.

That evening, the ugly bride resumed her place in the bridal chamber. When the prince asked her about the verses she had sung to the nettle bush and the church doors, she knew nothing. Suspicious, the prince searched the castle, found Maid Maleen washing dishes in the scullery, and saw the golden chain around her neck.

The truth was revealed. The treacherous pretender was banished, and the faithful Maid Maleen was crowned queen beside her overjoyed prince, proving that true constancy survives the deepest trials.
moral: True love endures darkness, stones, and humiliation, and truth shines through all deceit.

full_text:
A fearless discharged soldier wearing heavy boots of buffalo leather wandered through a dark forest when he met a stranger whose horse had broken its leg. The two men took shelter in an isolated hut, unaware that it was the den of a notorious band of bloodthirsty robbers.

An old woman guarding the hearth warned them that the robbers would soon return and slit their throats. While the stranger trembled in terror, the soldier calmly sat by the fire, smoked his pipe, and demanded roast pork and wine.

When the robber chief and twenty cutthroats stormed into the hut with drawn blades, the soldier did not flinch. "Welcome, brothers!" shouted the soldier. "Sit down and drink with us!"

When the robbers lunged to butcher them, the soldier drew his heavy sabre and fought with breathtaking fury, kicking with his stout buffalo boots and swinging his blade until he routed the ruffians, locking the survivors inside the cellar.

The soldier and his companion returned safely to the capital. There, the stranger revealed himself as the King! In recognition of the soldier's extraordinary bravery and loyalty, the King appointed him General of the Royal Guard, granting him lands and gold, while the veteran proudly wore his boots of buffalo leather to the finest royal banquets.
moral: Fearless bravery in the face of danger turns terrifying perils into triumph and honor.

full_text:
In the dead of winter, when deep snow covered the earth, a poor peasant boy was sent into the forest with a sledge to gather dry firewood. When his sledge was loaded, he felt so bitterly cold that he resolved to build a small fire before beginning the long trek home.

He cleared away the heavy snow to find bare ground. Scraping into the frozen earth, his hand struck something hard and metallic: a tiny, beautifully crafted key made of pure, sparkling gold.

Thinking that wherever there was a key there must surely be a lock, he dug deeper into the soil and uncovered an iron casket chased with delicate engravings. He searched eagerly around the box, but saw no keyhole upon the top or sides. At last, turning it over, he found an opening so small it could barely be seen.

He inserted the golden key into the tiny lock, and to his wonder, it fitted to perfection.

He turned the key in the lock... and now we must wait until he has fully unlocked the casket and opened the lid, so that we may see what wondrous and magnificent treasures lie hidden within.
moral: The greatest treasures of life and imagination are discovered when we turn the key of curiosity.

A wise king was renowned throughout the world because no secret remained hidden from him. Every evening at supper, after all dishes had been cleared, a trusted servant brought him a covered silver dish, which the king ate alone in absolute secrecy.

Overcome by curiosity, the servant carried the dish to a private room and lifted the lid. Inside lay a cooked white snake. Unable to resist, the servant took a single small bite. Instantly, he understood the speech of all living creatures: birds singing in the boughs, fish whispering beneath the waves, and ants murmuring in the moss!

Armed with this miraculous gift, the servant journeyed across the realm. Along the way, he saved three dying fish by tossing them back into the brook, spared the life of an ant king by steering his horse around an anthill, and fed starving ravens by giving them his own bread.

Arriving at the capital, he sought to win the hand of the king's daughter. The princess set three impossible tasks: to retrieve a golden ring cast into the deep ocean, to gather thousands of spilled millet seeds from the grass before sunrise, and to fetch the golden apple from the Tree of Life.

The grateful fish dived to the ocean floor and retrieved the ring; the thankful ants gathered every single millet seed; and the loyal ravens flew to the edge of the world to bring the golden apple. The amazed princess accepted his hand, and the compassionate youth became king, ruling in wisdom and harmony with all living things.
moral: Compassion extended to creatures of the earth, air, and water returns as a shield in time of need.

A poor fisherman caught a miraculous golden fish that promised him endless wealth and a palace if he spared its life. The fish instructed the fisherman to feed two scales to his wife, two to his mare, and bury two in the garden.

From this miracle were born twin golden boys, two golden foals, and two golden lilies grew in the garden. As the brothers grew, radiant as the sun, they resolved to ride out into the world to seek their fortunes.

The elder brother rode into a distant realm where he rescued a lovely maiden from a terrifying dragon and married her in great joy. But one day, hunting in the enchanted forest, he chased a white hind into an eerie thicket, where a wicked witch turned him and his golden hound into cold stone.

Back home, the younger brother saw the golden lily in the garden droop and wither, signaling that his brother was in mortal danger.

Mounting his golden steed, the younger twin rode like the wind into the enchanted forest. Seeing the petrified hound and his brother's stone likeness, he seized the wicked witch by the throat, forcing her to anoint the stone statues with magical water.

The elder brother and his hound awakened to warm life. The reunited brothers embraced with tears of joy, drove the dark shadows from the forest forever, and returned home to celebrate their enduring bond in peace and prosperity.
moral: Brotherly devotion overcomes dark enchantments and brings life back from cold stone.

title: The Fox and the Geese
summary: A cunning fox crept into a green meadow where a flock of plump, healthy geese were peacefully grazing. Licking his chops, the fox stepped into their midst and said, "I have arrived...
full_text:
A cunning fox crept into a green meadow where a flock of plump, healthy geese were peacefully grazing. Licking his chops, the fox stepped into their midst and said, "I have arrived at the perfect hour; you are all fat and tender, and I intend to devour every single one of you on the spot!"

The terrified geese cackled and fluttered their wings in panic. One brave goose, keeping her wits about her, stepped forward and said: "Noble Fox, we know we must perish, but grant us one small, reasonable favor before we die. Allow us to say one final prayer so that we may depart this world in peace, and afterward we will line up in an orderly row so you may eat the fattest first."

"Very well," agreed the fox smugly. "That is a pious request. Pray on, and I will wait."

The first goose began her prayer: "Ga! Ga! Ga!"

The second goose took up the chant: "Ga! Ga! Ga!"

The third and fourth joined in, and soon the entire flock was honking and cackling "Ga! Ga! Ga!" at the top of their lungs, never ceasing for a single second.

The fox sat patiently waiting for the prayer to finish, but the geese are still praying to this very hour, and until they stop, the fox must sit and listen, unable to taste a single bite!
moral: Quick thinking in the face of peril can buy time and foil the cruelest schemes.

title: The Fox and the Cat
summary: A proud fox met a humble grey cat in the forest and looked down upon her with haughty disdain. "Good day, mistress cat," sneered the fox. "How do you manage to survive in these dan...
full_text:
A proud fox met a humble grey cat in the forest and looked down upon her with haughty disdain. "Good day, mistress cat," sneered the fox. "How do you manage to survive in these dangerous times? How many clever arts and tricks do you possess?"

"I know only one single art," replied the cat modestly.

"Only one?" laughed the fox boastfully. "How pitiful! I am master of a hundred arts, and besides that, I possess a sack full of cunning tricks that can outwit any hunter or hound in the world!"

Just then, four ferocious hunting hounds came bounding through the thicket, barking fiercely, followed by hunters on swift horses.

In an instant, the cat used her one art: she sprang up the trunk of a tall birch tree and sat safely in the high branches, sheltered by the dense leaves. "Open your sack of tricks, master fox!" called the cat from above. "Use your hundred arts!"

The boastful fox darted this way and that, doubling back, leaping over ditches, and trying all hundred of his cunning tricks. But the hounds surrounded him, cut off his escape, and captured him in the briars.

Watching from her secure perch, the cat sighed: "Master Fox, all your hundred arts could not save your skin, while my single modest art has kept me safe and sound!"
moral: One reliable, practical skill is worth more than a hundred boastful tricks that fail in danger.

A queen gave birth to a prince endowed with the wondrous gift of wishing: whatever he wished for in his pure heart would instantly come to pass. But the treacherous royal huntsman stole the child away, smeared the sleeping queen's apron with blood, and told the king that wild wolves had devoured his son, causing the grief-stricken monarch to imprison the innocent queen in a dark tower.

The huntsman raised the boy in an isolated cottage, intending to use the lad's wishing powers for his own selfish glory. When the prince grew into youth, he wished for a lovely maiden as his companion, and an exquisite girl appeared.

When the huntsman demanded that the prince wish for royal crowns and gold, the wise youth saw the huntsman's dark treachery. The prince wished the wicked huntsman transformed into a black poodle with a golden collar, forced to eat raw coals.

Transforming the maiden into a fragrant pink carnation to keep her safe, the prince carried her in his pocket and returned to his father's palace, offering to serve as a humble gardener. He wished for the most miraculous blossoms to bloom in winter, captivating the entire court.

At a grand banquet, he revealed his true identity, restored the carnation to her radiant human form, and commanded the poodle to speak the truth before the court. The king wept bitter tears of repentance, embraced his long-lost son, released his faithful queen from the tower, and banished evil from the realm forever.
moral: The wishes of an innocent and pure heart possess miraculous power over all evil.

Grethel was a cheerful cook who wore shoes with red rosettes and loved good food and fine wine. Whenever her master ordered a pair of plump chickens roasted for an honored guest, Grethel basted them with butter, salted them with care, and turned them on the spit until they were golden and fragrant.

"When wine is opened, it must be drunk," Grethel said to herself, taking a healthy draught from the cellar cask. "And when roast fowl smells this divine, it is a mortal sin not to taste!" She nibbled a wing, found it exquisite, and soon ate the entire first chicken.

When the guest was late and the second chicken began to scorch, Grethel thought, "One chicken cannot sit alone upon the silver platter," and ate the second one as well!

Suddenly, the master ran into the kitchen shouting, "Grethel, the guest has arrived! Hurry, sharpen the carving knife!" The master seized his great knife and ran to the doorstep to hone it upon the whetstone.

Grethel dashed to the front door, whispered to the guest in horror: "Flee for your life, sir! My master invited you only to slice off both your ears with his carving knife; see how he whets the blade!"

The terrified guest turned and fled down the lane at full sprint. Grethel then ran back to her master, shouting: "Master, master! That insolent guest has snatched both your roasted chickens from the platter and is running off with them!"

The master ran after him, waving the carving knife and shouting: "Just one! Leave me just one!" But the guest ran all the faster, clutching his ears, while clever Grethel wiped her lips and laughed heartily by the hearth.
moral: A nimble wit and swift tongue can talk a cook out of the tightest scrape.

full_text:
A holy wanderer traveling the countryside visited a blacksmith's forge. Seeing the smith's aged father trembling with palsy, bent double with years, the wanderer took pity on the old man. He placed him gently into the roaring furnace coals, blew the bellows with rhythmic grace, and quenched him in a vat of pure spring water.

To the smith's astonishment, the ancient father emerged as a vigorous, handsome youth of twenty, glowing with health and vitality!

When the wanderer departed, the proud blacksmith thought to himself: "What a marvelous art! Why should I hammer horseshoes when I can make old folks young and charge a mountain of gold?"

He persuaded his frail, eighty-year-old mother-in-law to climb into the forge. The blacksmith piled on coal, pumped the bellows with frantic speed, and heated the furnace to white heat. The poor woman shrieked in agony, while the foolish smith blew harder, convinced the magic was taking effect.

When he hauled her out and plunged her into the water barrel, she lay scorched and blackened, barely clinging to life.

Just then, the holy wanderer returned, heard the lamentations, and miraculously restored the scorched woman to health. He sternly rebuked the arrogant blacksmith: "Do not meddle with mysteries beyond your understanding; stick to your anvil and let divine grace tend to mortal life!"
moral: Miraculous healing belongs to divine grace; foolish presumption leads to disaster.

full_text:
When the Creator fashioned all the animals of the earth, he created gentle sheep, strong horses, noble hounds, and industrious bees to bless and assist humankind in their daily labors.

An envious spirit, looking upon this peaceful harmony with spite, resolved to create creatures of his own. He formed the fierce wolf to devour the sheep, the stinging hornet to torment the horses, and the thorny thistle to choke the grain fields.

The Creator looked upon these wild creations with boundless wisdom. Rather than destroying them, he brought them into cosmic harmony: he gave the sheep a loyal shepherd and protective hounds to guard against the wolf; he gave the birds appetite to eat the hornets; and he decreed that the donkey should find sweet nourishment in the prickly thistles.

Thus, even creatures formed in malice were integrated into the grand tapestry of nature, showing that wisdom transforms all things into a higher order of balance and purpose.
moral: Every creature has its appointed place in the balance of creation, serving harmony.

full_text:
Two country laborers were walking toward the city market when one of them noticed a tiny speck of dust clinging to the shoulder of a passing traveler. He pointed and laughed loudly, mocking the traveler's untidy appearance before the entire crowd.

A wise elder sitting by the town gates overheard the mockery. He stepped forward and placed a massive wooden oak timber beam directly across the scorner's own neck, bending him double under its crushing weight.

"Why do you put this heavy beam upon my neck?" cried the struggling laborer in agony.

The elder answered with quiet authority: "You laugh at a tiny speck of dust on another man's shoulder, yet you are blind to the colossal timber of arrogance and pride that crushes your own soul. Learn to remove the beam from your own heart before you mock the speck in your neighbor's eye."

Humbled and ashamed, the laborer begged for forgiveness, learning that true dignity lies in self-reflection rather than malicious fault-finding.
moral: Examine your own massive flaws before presuming to critique the small errors of others.

full_text:
An ancient beggar woman, shivering in threadbare rags and hobbling on wooden crutches, walked through the snow to the gate of a wealthy farmer's manor, begging for a warm potato or a single coal to kindle her frozen hearth.

The farmer's cruel son stood by the roaring kitchen fire, eating roasted meats. Instead of handing her a crust, he set the ferocious yard hounds upon her and mocked her trembling hands.

The poor woman turned away in silence, weeping into the bitter winter wind. As she hobbled past the barn, the cold frost seemed to envelop the farm in an unnatural chill. Within an hour, a sudden spark flew from the farmer's chimney, setting the thatched roof ablaze.

The farmer and his selfish son scrambled to quench the flames, but the water wells were frozen solid, and their grand manor burned to the ground in an hour. Left with neither roof nor bread, the proud youth was forced to beg along the snowy highway, remembering too late that scorning the desperate invites cold ruin upon one's own house.
moral: He who neglects the suffering beggar hardens his own soul against the light.

In a poor mountain village, an honest widow lived with her twelve young sons in a tiny thatched cottage. Though they had little to eat beyond wild roots and spring water, her heart was open to all who knocked.

One stormy night, twelve weary wanderers arrived at her door, soaked by the freezing rain. The widow welcomed them warmly, dried their cloaks by the hearth, and shared her last loaf of barley bread among them, eating nothing herself.

Before departing at dawn, the eldest wanderer blessed the humble dwelling: "Because you shared your meager bread with weary souls, your twelve sons shall grow to become pillars of faith and righteousness, protected from all darkness."

Years later, the twelve sons grew into noble, courageous men who traversed the earth, healing the sick, comforting the afflicted, and spreading light to every corner of the world, their mother's humble charity blossoming into a universal blessing for all humanity.
moral: Generous hospitality toward weary travelers brings everlasting peace and heavenly protection.

full_text:
A sweet, delicate child lived with her widowed mother at the edge of a deep pine wood. The little girl was so gentle of spirit that wild birds rested upon her shoulders and woodland deer ate from her small palm.

One autumn afternoon, while gathering wild berries in a quiet glade, she met a child clothed in radiant white, who smiled and handed her a freshly bloomed wild rose, whispering: "When this rose opens fully, I will return to bring you to a garden of eternal blossoms."

The child brought the rose home and placed it in a glass of clear spring water. Week after week passed, and while autumn frost stripped the forest boughs bare, the rose remained fresh and green on her windowsill.

On a quiet winter morning, the mother entered the bedroom and found the magnificent rose fully opened in breathtaking fragrant splendor. Beside it, the little child lay sleeping serenely with a radiant smile upon her sweet face, having walked peacefully into the eternal gardens with the companion she had met in the woods.
moral: The purest innocence blooms like a sweet rose, untouched by the corruption of the world.

full_text:
Three sisters were sent into the deep forest to deliver bread to their father. The two eldest lost their way, found an old thatched hut occupied by an elderly sage and his domestic beasts—a hen, a rooster, and a cow. The selfish elder daughters demanded supper and comfortable beds, eating their fill while ignoring the hungry animals. The elderly host sent them down into a cold cellar for their callous arrogance.

The youngest daughter, gentle and observant, arrived at the hut on the third evening. Before she touched a single morsel of porridge, she greeted the animals affectionately, fed sweet grain to the birds, and carried an armful of fresh clover to the cow. She ensured their water trough was filled and stroked their heads with genuine love.

When morning dawned, she was awakened by the singing of courtiers. The rustic hut had transformed into a glorious crystal palace! The elderly sage was revealed as an enchanted prince, freed from a century-long curse because a maiden had appeared whose compassionate heart honored humble creatures before herself.

The grateful prince married the maiden in royal splendor, while her older sisters were released and sent home with a wise lesson in true courtesy and kindness.
moral: Those who show loving kindness to all creatures, big and small, unlock the greatest blessings of life.

title: The Old Man and Grandson variant
summary: An old grandfather lived with his son and daughter-in-law. His eyesight was dim, his hearing was faint, and his hands trembled so violently with age that he often spilled soup upon...
keywords: the old man and grandson variant
full_text:
An old grandfather lived with his son and daughter-in-law. His eyesight was dim, his hearing was faint, and his hands trembled so violently with age that he often spilled soup upon the tablecloth or dropped his spoon.

Disgusted by the mess, the cold-hearted daughter-in-law made the old grandfather sit in the corner behind the stove, serving his food in a cheap earthenware bowl while the family dined merrily at the main table. The old man sat in silence, tears rolling down his weathered cheeks.

One day, his trembling hands dropped the earthenware bowl, and it shattered upon the flagstones. The woman scolded him bitterly and bought him a rough wooden trough for two farthings, forcing him to eat his meals like a barnyard beast.

A few days later, the parents saw their four-year-old son sitting on the floor, busily carving small pieces of wood with his father's chisel.

"What are you making there, little one?" asked the father fondly.

The little boy looked up with innocent eyes and replied, "I am making a little wooden trough for you and mother to eat out of when you grow old, just like grandfather!"

The parents looked at each other in stunned silence. Overwhelmed by shame and grief, they burst into tears. They walked to the stove, took the old grandfather gently by the hand, led him to the place of honor at the head of the table, and treated him with loving reverence for all the remaining days of his life.
moral: Treat your elders with tenderness and dignity, for your children will follow your example.

A little brother and sister were playing beside a deep forest well when they both slipped and tumbled into the water. At the bottom, a cruel Water Nixie seized them, dragging them to her subterranean dwelling.

"Now you shall work for me!" cackled the Nixie. She gave the girl tangled dirty flax to spin and a leaky bucket to carry water, while the boy was forced to chop heavy stone with a blunt wooden axe, giving them only sour turnip peels to eat.

One Sunday, while the Nixie went to the village church, the children seized their chance and fled toward the upper world.

When the Nixie discovered their escape, she pursued them with furious, watery strides, surging like a tidal wave across the meadow.

The little girl threw a brush behind her; it instantly transformed into a towering mountain of bristling spikes, slowing the Nixie down.

When the Nixie climbed over, the boy tossed a comb behind them; it turned into a vast mountain of thousands of sharp teeth, halting the Nixie's charge once more.

Finally, as the Nixie drew near, the girl dropped a small pocket mirror; it expanded into a colossal, sheer mountain of slippery glass! The Nixie could not climb the smooth surface, slipped back into the depths, and the clever children returned safely to their parents' warm embrace.
moral: Quick wits and clever obstacles outrun the grasp of cruel enchantments.

A cock and a hen went up to the Nut Hill to gather hazelnuts, agreeing to share everything they found. But when the hen found a colossal nut, she swallowed it whole out of greed, and the giant shell lodged in her throat.

"Hurry, dear cock!" gasped the hen. "Run to the well and fetch water, or I will choke to death!"

The cock ran to the well, but the well demanded a wreath of silk from the bride. The bride demanded a garland of willow from the willow tree. The willow demanded a ribbon from the maiden. The cock ran frantically from one to another, fulfilling every demand with loyal devotion.

By the time he returned to the Nut Hill with the cool spring water, the hen had already choked and lay lifeless upon the grass.

Overcome by grief, the faithful cock built a funeral car, harnessed six mice, and conveyed the departed hen to her grave. A fox, a wolf, and a bear asked to ride along in mourning. But when the heavy car reached the rushing river, the bridge gave way, and the mourning party plunged into the deep stream, leaving the grieving cock to mourn his lost companion in lonely sorrow.
moral: Selfish disregard for warnings brings sorrow, while faithful comrades mourn together.

Along the road, he met Saint Peter disguised as a poor beggar. Lustig shared his last coins and bread with cheerful generosity. In gratitude, Saint Peter granted him a magical knapsack: whatever Lustig commanded to enter the knapsack was bound to jump inside immediately!

When Lustig stopped at an inn, he ordered roasted geese from the air into his knapsack and dined like a king. Later, he arrived at a haunted castle where terrifying demons tormented the region. Lustig stepped inside, waited until the demons attempted to tear him apart, and shouted: "Into the knapsack, all of you!"

The howling demons tumbled into the sack. Lustig carried the heavy knapsack to the village blacksmith, laid it upon the anvil, and had the smith hammer it with his heaviest sledgehammer until the demons screamed for mercy and swore never to torment mortal souls again!

When his life's journey ended, Lustig marched up to the pearly gates. Saint Peter hesitated to admit the rowdy wanderer, but Lustig tossed his knapsack over the golden threshold and shouted, "I wish myself inside my knapsack!" Instantly, he found himself inside heaven, laughing heartily and greeting the angels with cheerful comradeship.
moral: A merry heart and unshakeable good cheer overcome all trials and turn every obstacle into joy.

full_text:
Hansel was a gambler who played cards and rolled dice from dawn till dusk, losing his coat, his boots, and his father's cottage, yet his cheerful passion for gaming never diminished.

When he gave shelter to a wandering pilgrim, he was granted a magical apple tree from which no one could climb down without Hansel's permission, and a deck of cards that never lost a wager.

When Death came with his scythe to take Hansel away, Hansel said courteously: "Dear Death, before we depart, would you kindly climb my apple tree and pick me one sweet apple for the journey?"

Death climbed into the tree, and immediately became stuck fast to the boughs! For seven long years, Death sat trapped in the tree; no one on earth died, no sickness was fatal, and humanity lived in endless merriment.

Finally, Hansel bargained with Death: he would release him only if Death promised never to claim him until Hansel called for him.

Years later, when Hansel wearied of mortal life, he journeyed to the underworld, pulled out his magical cards, and won games against every spirit in the halls, winning countless souls and leading them in a joyful procession straight into paradise, proving that an unyielding spirit laughs at fate itself.
moral: Sharp wits that refuse defeat can turn even the final judgment into a spirited game of dice.

full_text:
A king's daughter gave birth to a child, but no one knew who the father was. The king gathered all the noble lords and princes of the kingdom and gave the baby a golden lemon, proclaiming that whoever the infant gave the fruit to was his father.

To everyone's shock, the child bypassed all the gilded dukes and handed the golden lemon to Hans Dumb, a simple, hunchbacked youth whom everyone mocked. Furious at the disgrace, the king sealed Hans, the princess, and the child inside a wooden barrel and cast them into the ocean swell.

 Hans Dumb possessed a miraculous gift: whatever he wished came to pass. Floating in the dark barrel, he wished it transformed into a luxurious golden vessel with silk sails. He wished for a magnificent palace on an enchanted island, and an imperial estate appeared with fountains and rose gardens.

He then wished himself transformed into a handsome, wise prince of extraordinary grace.

Years later, the old king visited the island, marveling at the glorious realm. When the host revealed himself as Hans Dumb and introduced his daughter and grandson, the humbled king fell to his knees in repentance, recognizing that divine blessing chooses the humble over the proud.
moral: The simple and overlooked often hold the secret keys to royal fortune.

title: The Three Brothers variant
summary: An aging father possessed a cottage and could not decide which of his three sons should inherit it, as he loved them all equally. He told them: "Go out into the world and learn a t...
full_text:
An aging father possessed a cottage and could not decide which of his three sons should inherit it, as he loved them all equally. He told them: "Go out into the world and learn a trade. Whoever demonstrates the greatest mastery of his craft shall have the house."

The eldest became a barber, the second a blacksmith, and the youngest a fencing master. They returned home after three years to demonstrate their skills.

As they sat before the cottage, a swift hare ran across the meadow. The eldest son, the barber, lathered soap while running beside the bounding hare and shaved its whiskers completely clean without cutting its skin or slowing its pace!

Next, a nobleman galloped past in a four-horse carriage at full speed. The second son, the blacksmith, ran alongside, unbolted four worn horseshoes and forged and nailed four brand-new iron shoes onto the galloping hooves without causing the horse to break its stride!

Finally, a sudden cloudburst poured heavy rain from the sky. The youngest son, the swordsman, drew his rapier and twirled it above his head with such breathtaking speed that not a single raindrop touched his clothes; he stood dry as if sheltered beneath a copper roof!

The amazed father laughed with joy: "You have all displayed impossible mastery!" Rather than separate, the three brothers lived together in the cottage in lifelong harmony, sharing their prosperity and craft in mutual love.
moral: Supreme mastery of one’s craft and peaceful brotherhood are the truest inheritance.

title: The Devil and Grandmother variant

full_text:
Three soldiers deserted a cruel army and hid in a standing cornfield. Surrounded by guards and facing starvation, they accepted an offer from a dark winged dragon: he would carry them to safety and provide them with an endless purse of gold for seven years. But if, at the end of the term, they could not solve three riddles, their souls were forfeit.

For seven years, the three soldiers lived generously, feeding the hungry and enjoying life. As the final day approached, two of the soldiers wept in terror.

The third soldier, brave and cunning, walked into a desolate mountain gorge and found an ancient grandmother sitting spinning by a hearth. Seeing his upright heart, she agreed to help him. She hid him behind the chimney and eavesdropped when her devil grandson returned.

The proud devil boasted to his grandmother: "Those foolish soldiers will never guess my riddles! What is the roast meat? A dead ape in a silver dish! What is the wine? Lake water in an iron flask! What is the silver spoon? The jawbone of a wild boar!"

The soldier memorized the answers. When the demon arrived to claim their souls, the three soldiers answered each riddle with laughing confidence. Defeated and humiliated, the devil fled with a shriek into the abyss, leaving the three brave soldiers to enjoy their boundless gold in freedom and honor.
moral: Courage and resourcefulness can outsmart the craftiest traps and save comrades from doom.

Two boys were born in the same hour: Ferdinand Faithful and Ferdinand Unfaithful. When they grew into youth, they rode out into the world. Ferdinand Faithful found a talking white horse named Falada, who advised him with magical wisdom, and a magical feather that glowed with celestial light.

Ferdinand Faithful entered the service of the King, who favored him for his honest diligence. Envious of his favor, Ferdinand Unfaithful plotted his ruin, whispering to the King that Ferdinand Faithful boasted he could retrieve the lost princess from the Castle of the Sun, or bring back the sunken crown from the sea.

Under the counsel of his talking steed, Ferdinand Faithful embarked on these perilous quests. He fed meat to giant ravens, tossed bread to starving fishes, and used enchanted mirrors to pacify mythical beasts.

The grateful ravens retrieved the royal crown from the ocean abyss, and the faithful youth brought back the radiant princess.

When Ferdinand Unfaithful attempted to take credit for the miracles, the talking horse exposed his lies before the assembled court. The false companion was banished, and Ferdinand Faithful married the radiant princess, ruling the kingdom in justice, peace, and eternal loyalty.
moral: Faithful integrity overcomes the treacherous plots of envious rivals.

full_text:
A princess lost in a dark, tangled forest found an iron stove standing among the trees. From within the iron grate, a sorrowful voice spoke: "I am a king's son under a sorcerer's enchantment. If you promise to marry me and return to deliver me, I will show you the path home."

The princess escaped, but her father sent false miller's daughters in her place; the iron stove detected the deceit instantly. Finally, the true princess returned, scraped through the iron shell with a pocket knife, and released the handsome prince.

Before their wedding, the prince stepped aside to visit his parents, but forgot his bride when an enchanted kiss broke his memory.

The abandoned princess walked across the world to find him. She traversed a mountain of sharp needles, climbed three sheer peaks of ice, and crossed a lake of burning pitch, guided by gifts of golden spinning wheels and golden combs given to her by the four winds.

Reaching the prince's palace on the eve of his marriage to a false bride, she bought three nights in his chamber with her golden treasures. On the third night, the prince avoided the sleeping draught, heard her weeping songs of the iron stove, and recognized his true deliverer. The false bride was dismissed, and the faithful lovers reigned in everlasting joy.
moral: True devotion endures needles of steel and mountains of glass to deliver the beloved.

full_text:
A peasant woman named Catherine was so exceedingly lazy that whenever she was supposed to spin flax into thread, she spun it so poorly that the reel was full of knots. When her husband scolded her for not winding the yarn onto a reel, Catherine had a ready excuse: "How can I wind yarn when we have no wooden reel? Go into the forest and chop timber to make me one!"

The husband went into the forest to chop hazel wood for a reel. Catherine secretly ran ahead, hid in a thicket, and sang in an eerie voice: "He who cuts wood for a reel shall choke to death; he who winds yarn shall never draw breath!"

Terrified that the forest spirits were warning him of mortal danger, the husband dropped his axe and ran home, swearing never to speak of a reel again.

Next, Catherine placed the tangled boiled yarn into a pot with an old dead sparrow. When the husband asked for his dinner, he pulled out the bird. "See!" cried Catherine. "Even the pot knows that yarn should not be wound; the thread has turned into a feathered bird!"

The gullible husband marveled at the wonder, swore off linen altogether, and Catherine sat merrily by the fire, laughing at how easily a sharp tongue and a little cunning can turn lazy hours into peaceful rest.
moral: A clever rogue can invent endless excuses to avoid work, but true prosperity comes from honest effort.
